pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. ## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools … [truncated]

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

## zotero-research
Read-only access to the user's Zotero research library. For substantive sport-science questions, build a Zotero-first evidence pack before answering. Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. SecondBrain Queue is the priority lane; promotion eligibility is controlled by promotion_scope.

# AGENTS.md

Working instructions for any AI agent in this repo. Project-specific context lives in
`CLAUDE.md` at the repo root and in `docs/context.md`. Read both before starting.

## Who this is for

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. 14 varsity sports,
325+ student-athletes. Reports to Chris Ruf; Kenny Boyd is Executive Senior Associate AD.

## Writing rules

These are not stylistic suggestions. Drafts that break them get sent back.

- No em dashes. Use a comma, a colon, or a new sentence.
- No corporate jargon, no promotional language, no AI-sounding phrasing.
- Plain language throughout, even for technical topics. Audiences are mixed and not
  uniformly technical.
- Lead with the answer, then the reasoning. Pyramid Principle, not a procedural walk-up.
- Concise by default. Short answers over long breakdowns unless depth is asked for.
- Explain history and concepts at roughly a college freshman level.
- Run finished documents through the `humanizer` and `articulation` skills before delivery.

## Document standards

All documents use the Baylor design system:

| Element | Value |
|---|---|
| Baylor green | `#154734` |
| University gold | `#FFB81C` |
| Warm paper background | `#faf8f3` |
| Display face | Fraunces |
| Body face | IBM Plex Sans |
| Labels / mono | JetBrains Mono |

The full spec lives in the "Brand & Design System" section of
`07_EDUCATION/2026_AppliedNewsletter/CLAUDE.md` on the primary storage drive.

Deliverables should be complete and ready to use, not outlines. A full .docx or .pptx,
not a description of one.

## File handling

- **Always create new files. Never overwrite an existing one.** Version with a new name.
- Default to 2025 as the current year in documents, unless the project says otherwise.
  Exception: anything under MatchupAnalysis_FB2026 / Weekly_Matchups_2026 uses real 2026
  dates and 2026 data.
- Keep third-party platforms read-only. Navigate and read; do not edit anything there.
- Never paste API keys or credentials into chat. Read them from files on disk and never
  echo the value.

## Tooling

- Prefer Desktop Commander over Windows MCP whenever both could do the job.
- Document generation: `docx` (Node) for Word, `pptxgenjs` for PowerPoint.
- Data: Python, R, DuckDB, Power BI, React/TypeScript, FastAPI, Excel.
- Kitman Labs is the athlete management system.

### pptxgenjs failure modes

- No `#` prefix on hex colors
- Shadow objects need factory functions, not reused references
- No unicode bullets
- Do not combine `lineSpacing` with bulleted text

### docx-js patterns

- Hex colors without `#`
- Column widths in DXA units
- Separate numbering reference IDs per section

## Repo conventions

One folder per project under `~/DEV` (`C:\DEV` on the Windows machine), with `CLAUDE.md`
at the root and a `docs/` folder. Durable notes get written to `docs/` and committed,
never left only in a cloud project. Each project is its own git repo, private on GitHub
under `erash11`.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.
# Performance Playbook

Reusable Word and PowerPoint templates for the Baylor Applied Performance intern
training curriculum. The point is standardized, adaptable templates that deliver
consistent curriculum across program cycles, not one-off documents.

## Technologies covered

Force plates, GPS monitoring, velocity-based training, heart rate analysis, and
tensiomyography, taught inside a structured learning framework.

## The two templates

**SOP template (Word).** Two-column format with visual hierarchy: dark headers and
color-coded text, red for warnings and blue for notes. Covers the technology lifecycle
end to end, from setup through data management.

**Presentation template (PowerPoint).** Baylor official colors, green `#154734` and
gold `#FFB81C`, with approved typography. Structured as a 16-week curriculum framework
covering both technical and soft skills.

## Standards

Two-column layouts, consistent visual hierarchy, and placeholder systems so a template
can be customized quickly for a new technology. Clemson's program is the structural
reference; Baylor's brand standards govern everything visual.

## Caution

The workbooks and decks here are large binary files (33 MB across 5 files). Commit a
new version on structural change, not on every content edit.

## Related

- Intern_Curriculum (the curriculum these templates deliver)
- Education_Alignment_Initiative (Performance School, the staff-facing track)

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute
entries.description:
Run multiple commands in ONE call. Every command's output is auto-indexed into the knowledge base; if you also pass `queries`, the matching sections come back in the same round trip so a follow-up search call is not needed.

Concurrency parallelizes the FETCH phase (run-the-commands). The DERIVATION phase — turning raw output into an answer — still belongs in code: add a processing command that consumes the indexed output and prints only the answer, so the raw bytes never enter your conversation (Think-in-Code, same principle as the sandbox tool).

WHEN:
  - You have 3+ related commands you would otherwise run sequentially (multi-issue lookups, git log + git diff + git blame, multi-file reads, multi-region cloud queries)
  - You want to gather AND query in one round trip — pass `queries` so the matching sections come back inline
  - You want to parallelize I/O-bound work — pass `concurrency` 2-8 (network calls, gh CLI, cloud APIs, multi-repo git reads)
  - The combined output is large enough that piping it through ctx_search later would itself be expensive — let auto-index + inline queries do both in one shot

WHEN NOT:
  - Single command with no follow-up query — run it in the sandbox tool directly
  - CPU-bound or stateful commands — keep concurrency at 1 (npm test, build, lint, port-binding servers, lock-file holders, anything that races on the same resource)

RETURNS:
  Auto-indexed section list per command label, plus top matches per query (when `queries` is passed). Raw output is NOT echoed in full — only the matched windows. Concurrency>1 switches each command to its own per-command timeout (no shared budget); concurrency=1 preserves the legacy shared-budget cascading-skip-on-timeout path. Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches; keep at 1 for CPU work or shared-state commands; lower the value when target hosts enforce per-IP rate limits.

EXAMPLE: ctx_batch_execute(
  commands: [
    {label: "issue 1", command: "gh issue view 1"},
    {label: "issue 2", command: "gh issue view 2"},
    {label: "summarize", command:… [truncated]

label.description: Section header for this command's output (e.g., 'README', 'Package.json', 'Source Tree')

commands.description: Commands to execute as a batch. Output is labeled with the section header. Default order is sequential; pass concurrency>1 to run in parallel (output stays in input order).

queries.description: Search queries to extract information from indexed output. Use 5-8 comprehensive queries. Each returns top 5 matching sections with full content. This is your ONLY chance — put ALL your questions here. No follow-up calls needed.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs. With concurrency=1, the value (when set) is a shared budget across commands; with concurrency>1, it is applied per-command.

concurrency.description: Max commands to run in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches (network, gh, curl, multi-repo git reads). Keep at 1 for CPU-bound (npm test, build, lint) or stateful commands (ports, locks). >1 switches to per-command timeouts (no shared budget) and individual `(timed out)` blocks instead of cascading skip.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for all shell commands in this batch.

query_scope.description: Scope for `queries` (default: `batch`). `batch` searches ONLY the chunks produced by this batch's commands — useful when you want answers about the just-fetched output. `global` searches the entire persistent index (same scope as ctx_search) — useful when you want the batch commands to enrich context and the queries to also surface related prior knowledge in one round trip.

entries.description:
Read a file into a sandboxed FILE_CONTENT variable and run code over it. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation — the file bytes stay in the sandbox.

Think-in-Code applied to file-level analysis: Reading the whole file means every byte enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. Running code over it here lets you keep the raw bytes out and only the derived answer in. Same principle as ctx_execute, scoped to one named file via the FILE_CONTENT variable.

WHEN:
  - You want to KNOW SOMETHING ABOUT a file (line count, matches of a pattern, parsed structure, statistical aggregate) without needing to SEE all of it

  - The file is large enough that reading the full content would burn meaningful conversation memory you need for the actual work

WHEN NOT:

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
entries.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-… [truncated]

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

project.description: Project scope. Default (omit): this session's project — auto-resolved from the host adapter. 'global': span every project in the shared store (cross-project recall). <absolute-path>: scope to that specific project directory.

7	## [Heading 1] SECTION 1: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

10	Table of of Contents 
11	1. Why Assessments 
12	2. Speciﬁc vs General Tests 
13	3. Validity & Reliability 
14	4. Detecting Change 
15	5. Reassessment 
16	6. Gender Differences 
17	7. Team Cultures and Assessments 
18	8. Iowa Sport Assessment Table 
19	9. Common Assessments 
20	
21	
22	===== PAGE 3 =====
23	3
24	Why Assessments? 
25	“The primary aim of testing is to obtain information that assists the coach in creating an in-
26	dividual plan for each athlete. It is, of course, true that testing an athlete can help to moti-
27	vate both athlete and practitioner or support the eﬃcacy of a particular training method, 
28	but these outcomes should be considered secondary to the primary aim of GAINING IN-
29	FORMATION that informs the practitioner’s training program design.”   
30	 Jeremy Sheppard and Tim Gabbett  
31	Speciﬁc Tests vs General Tests 
32	Sport speciﬁc tests have utility with the assessment process, but rarely is the strength & condi-
33	tioning coach grading or assessing such processes. Typically, the goal of the strength & condi-
34	tioning coach is to utilize more general tests that provide the some of the underpinning deter-
35	minants of such speciﬁc tasks in sports. 
36	An example is the vertical jump seen in basketball, volleyball, and diving. The vertical jump 
37	outcomes may be similar across athletes, but the underpinnings of vertical jump relate to im-
38	pulse (Force x Time). So an athlete would need to examine the maximal force production abili-
39	ty, and also tasks that require force developed rapidly. IMTP , Back Squat, Deadlift for maximal 
40	strength, and ballistic exercises such as cleans, snatches, jump squats for explosive strength 
41	may provide a clearer picture of where an athlete needs to spend time to enhance their vertical 
42	jump performance.
43	
44	
45	===== PAGE 4 =====
46	4
47	Validity 
48	A valid test measures what it is intended to measure (and is considered suﬃciently reliable to 
49	use).
50	Types of Validity 
51	●	Ecological: refers to how well the assessment tool relates to actual athlete perfor-
52	mance and how well the ﬁndings can be applied in real-life settings.
53	●	Construct: refers to the overall validity, or the extend to which the test actually mea-
54	sures what it is designed to measure.
55	●	Face: is the appearance to the athlete, coach, and other practitioners that the test 
56	measures what it is purported to measure.
57	●	Content: refers to the expert assessment that the monitoring tool measures what it 
58	claims to measure.
59	●	Criterion: refers to the relationship between the scores on the test and scores on a cri-
60	terion measure. Criterion measure is a test that is widely accepted as a gold-standard 
61	and valid test. E.g. Force plates for force testing vs deriving force from a displacement 
62	sensor (e.g. Gymaware).
63	●	Concurrent: refers to the validity of a test for measuring a construct at a particular 
64	time. In most cases, the test is correlated with another, more accurate measure of the 
65	construct that is not feasible in most sport situations (e.g. Doing a 3km time trail on the 
66	day of competition)
67	●	Predictive: refers to the ability of a test to predict some construct or outcome in the 
68	future.
69	
70	===== PAGE 5 =====
71	5
72	Reliability 
73	The reliability of a measure (test) can be viewed simply as the amount of variation that occurs 
74	from one test occasion to another.
75	Learning eﬀect: Athletes should have at least 3-4 familiarization trials to reduce any learning 
76	eﬀects. For instance, before performing an isometric-mid-thigh-pull (IMTP) assessment, the 
77	athlete(s) should get accustomed to the position of pulling, the use of straps, and sensation 
78	prior to the real assessment. If you're ﬁnding yourself having to coach the task quite a bit, the 
79	athlete will likely experience improvements the next time they assess simply by the learning ef-
80	fect.
81	Types of Reliability 
82	1.	Interrater reliability: refers to the degree to which diﬀerent people conducting the as-
83	sessment agree in their test results over time or on repeated occasions.
84	2.	Intrarater reliability: refers to the consistency of scores in repeated tests conducted by 
85	a single tester.
86	Detecting Change 
87	The sensitivity of a assessment (or even a monitoring) tool refers to its ability to detect small 
88	but important changes in performance or an aspect such as fatigue. 
89	Meaningful change is deﬁned as the smallest practical change that is important. 
90	To ensure meaningful change is occurring, please allow the Sports Science depart-
91	ment to help provide you (the S&C coach) insight into this area as this is beyond this 
92	manual at this time. 
93	
94	
95	===== PAGE 6 =====
96	6
97	Reassessment 
98	Reassessment is primarily dependent upon three factors:
99	●	Time within the competition year. There is a contextual evaluation that must occur to 
100	ensure proper placement of assessments. This is especially more important the closer 
101	one is to the competition period.
102	●	The expectation of change. If you are in a maximal strength phase  for a beginner or in-
103	termediate athlete, you may consider reassessing in 4 weeks. If the athlete is and ad-
104	vanced athlete, you may consider a longer period. This is also dependent upon the 
105	length of the phase. The length of training period would extend the reassessment date 
106	to allow for adequate recovery to occur.
107	●	Unexpected recovery issues. Do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue. A big 
108	reason for reassessment is to provide the athlete the conﬁdence they are improving. 
109	Ensure their readiness matches their assessment needs. This may require multiple as-
110	sessment dates for a team sport, or a larger group of individuals. Be ﬂexible.
111	Gender Differences 
112	The primary consideration here is the female menstrual cycle. To complicate matters more, if a 
113	female is utilizing birth control, there are a  number of variables that are diﬃcult to control for. 
114	In general, the two primary phases of the menstrual cycle that a practitioner should be aware 
115	of is the follicular and the luteal phase. 
116	The follicular phase is the ﬁrst phase of the menstrual cycle. This phase has the association of 
117	an increase of testosterone and estrogen. In terms of adaptability of training stressors, women 
118	that perform more strength/power/speed based work during this phase may adapt better. This 
119	may also be the same for the assessment of strength/power/speed.
120	The luteal phase is the second phase of the menstrual cycle. This phase has the association 
121	with a decrease of testosterone, estrogen, and the increase of progesterone. In terms of adapt-
122	===== PAGE 7 =====
123	7
124	ability of training stressors, women's that perform more endurance based work during this 
125	phase may adapt better. This may also be the same for the assessment of endurance.
126	Considerations and reality. 
127	Ideally, you and the medical staﬀ are aware of your female student-athletes menstrual cycle 
128	history, length, and even medications. This may help aide in training design and assessment 
129	procedures. 
130	In reality, most will not have access to this. And even though if available, in team sports, this 
131	may never enter into the decision making processes. 
132	 In summary, team communication and transparency, monitoring procedures, 
133	relationships, and general sound heuristics should drive your decision making. If you feel 
134	an athlete's readiness is not going to match the requirements for assessment then 
135	consider postponing. 
136	Team Cultures and Assessments 
137	There will be a number of speciﬁc and even general assessments that you may likely never do 
138	because they are already happening within sport practice already. This doesn’t necessarily 
139	mean you dismiss the assessments, but you can use their information to help triangulate what 
140	you’re seeing to come up with possible valuable insight to the athlete and coaching staﬀ. Addi-
141	tionally, in regards to meaningful change, this is where you can employ help from the Sports 
142	Science staﬀ to help give your coaching staﬀ(s) more conﬁdence there was actual change that 
143	they can be conﬁdent with.
144	
145	
146	===== PAGE 8 =====
147	8
148	Athlete Preparation Before Testing 
149	The preparation instructions ensure two things
150	●	The student-athlete is in the best possible condition prior to their assessment(s)
151	●	To ensure test to test reliability
152	Instructions: 
153	●	Diet: 
154	◦	Athletes should be encourage to consume a series of high-carbohydrate meals in 
155	the 36 hours prior to testing and arrive on test day well hydrated.
156	◦	No food or caﬀeine are to be consumed in the 2 hours prior to testing
157	●	Training: 
158	◦	No training inducing severe physiological or neural fatigue should be undertaken in 
159	48-72 hours prior to testing. This includes any high-intensity skill training as well.
160	●	Testing:
161	◦	All test sessions should be scheduled at the same time of day (ideally) to avoid 
162	ﬂuctuations in physioloigcal response to set procotrols due to circadian rhythm. All 
163	tests must be completed in the recommended standarized order with adequate 
164	and consistent recovery tiem between tests. This will promote optimal perfor-
165	mance and allow for valid comparison of results on diﬀerent test occasions.
166	
167

169	9
170	Iowa Sport Assessment Table 
171	 
172	 
173

175	===== PAGE 10 =====
176	10
177	General Assessments 
178	Physical Competency Assessment (PCA) 
179	Description: The Physical Competency Assessment is a S&C developed global assessment to 
180	give fundamental information regarding the preparedness to train. Preparedness to compete is 
181	not being assessed here. This assessment will always be done with a battery of physical based 
182	assessments (e.g. mechanical power testing) and non-physical assessments (e.g. TMG, Ome-
183	gawave).
184	Frequency of Testing: There should be a minimal of ONE time per year where this assessment 
185	should be performed. The most impactful time(s) is when your student-athletes have been 
186	away from campus for an extended period of time and/or after the competition season.
187	Consider retesting "at risk" exercises more frequently if you are actively working to-
188	wards modifying the risk (e.g. Large single leg squat deﬁcit) 
189	Validity & Reliability: This assessment has been formulated by the Strength & Conditioning 
190	department. In general, we are not aware of the reliability and validity of the assessment. But 
191	general heuristics would tell us it is a means to an end, and helps foster unknown intelligence 
192	regarding a student-athlete by not necessarily the tests themselves, but with the conversations 
193	that follow.
194	Anthropometrics 
195	Description: Anthropometrics have a strong association with success for most sports. There 
196	are certain heights, weights, limb lengths, and muscle/fat ratios that appear to help optimize 
197	performance outcomes. 
198	Frequency of Testing: 
199	●	Height: 1x
200	●	Limb lengths: 1x
201	
202	===== PAGE 11 =====
203	11
204	●	Bodyweight: Weekly
205	●	Body composition (if available via scanning/measuring): No more than 4x / year
206	●	Body composition (skin fold sums): BI-monthly or monthly
207	Validity & Reliability: The assessment of height, limb lengths, and bodyweight are valid and 
208	reliable. The scales that we utilized at Iowa are tested around 2x per year. Body composition is 
209	a valid tool, but the typical error in the “best” devices can still be as low as +/-4%. Meaning, if 
210	you your body composition and review the body fat % value and its 15%, the actual range you 
211	would fall between 11-19%. So if the athlete changes their behaviors to induce a body fat drop 
212	and they re-test, and it says 15% again, can you be certain they didn’t get any leaner? No, be-
213	cause they could have gotten leaner (perhaps you can visually see, their bodyweight has 
214	dropped), but they were simply a victim of typical error which is a function of technology vari-
215	ation and biological variation. So, you need to utilize other information to best deliver your 
216	analysis.
217	
218	
219	===== PAGE 12 =====
220	12
221	Jump Assessments 
222	Counter Movement Jump 
223	Description: The counter movement jump (CMJ) oﬀers a lot of insight about the athletes per-
224	formance abilities by itself, when used in combination with other tests, and is a useful tool to 
225	gauge compensatory patterns (when using the force plate), and can be a valid tool to monitor 
226	neuromuscular fatigue.
227	How to Test:
228	●	Stand on the jump mat or force plate with hands on hips. 
229	●	Instruct the athlete to simply jump as high as possible. Do not coach strategy of jump-
230	ing.
231	●	Instruct the athlete to land with a stiﬀ and stable landing. This is important to gauge 
232	appropriate jump height and also peak landing force when on the force plate.
233	●	 Have athlete perform 3 jumps.
234	Frequency of testing:
235	●	Asymmetry analysis: 1x / month, unless athlete has rich injury history or is coming 
236	back from an injury
237	●	Peak concentric force (for Dynamic Strength Index (DSI)): Whenever you feel there is a 
238	need to ﬁnd their new DSI to make appropriate interventional changes. During the oﬀ-
239	season, this is appropriate before and after each training phase. Suggestion Utilize 
240	DSI more frequently with your more developed athletes as most underdeveloped ath-
241	letes simply need a good mixed program, and likely one that favors strength develop-
242	ment over other forms of training (e.g. speed, power)
243	●	Jump Height: Weekly or Before and after training phases. Depends on your purpose. If 
244	you are going weekly, you will want to utilize the AVERAGE jump height across 3 
245	===== PAGE 13 =====
246	13
247	jumps. This appears to be a valid form of neuromuscular fatigue monitoring. If you are 
248	testing before and after training phases, and jump height is a key performance indica-
249	tor (e.g. basketball, volleyball, diving), then you should gauge the improvement of this if 
250	that is being targeted. For instance, after a maximal strength phase with a more devel-
251	oped athlete, jump height may go down as there still is residual fatigue. In a lesser de-
252	veloped athlete, it may go up after any form of training. So it is critical to contextual 
253	frame the outcomes for your athletes.
254	Jump height when using it for monitoring (average of 3 jumps), KPI monitoring, 
255	or it’s inclusion into the Eccentric Utilization Ratio (EUR) analysis can be all done 
256	on the contact mat. 
257	●	 RSImod: Weekly, especially during in-season or phases of training where you feel the 
258	speed and technical demand is high. Since RSImod is an eﬃciency metric, it can pro-
259	vide you insight of the jump strategy in relation to the ﬂight time. This output is provid-
260	ed via the ForceDecks software. 
261	Equipment:
262	●	Contact Mat (only for Jump Height), Force Plate (Asymmetry, Jump Height, Peak Con-
263	centric Force, RSImod)
264	 Squat Jump 
265	Description: The squat jump (SJ) is similar to the CMJ, but minus the eccentric (or lowering) 
266	phase of the CMJ. This is to help determine the athlete’s ability to utilize their stretch shorten-
267	ing cycle (SSC) in the jumping pattern, more specially the Slow SSC function which is more as-
268	sociated with larger joint angles specially around the knee and hip joints.
269	How to Test:
270	●	Stand on the jump mat or force plate with hands on hips. 
271	●	Instruct the athlete to lower down into the bottom of their CMJ position and pause in 
272	that position for 3-4 seconds. This time is necessary to remove much of the SSC con-
273	centric contribution.
274	
275	===== PAGE 14 =====
276	14
277	●	Upon command, Instruct the athlete to simply jump as high as possible without dip-
278	ping down.
279	●	Instruct the athlete to land with a stiﬀ and stable landing. This is important to gauge 
280	appropriate jump height and also peak landing force when on the force plate.
281	●	 Have athlete perform 3 jumps.
282	●	This test is more suitable on the contact mat because of the high sensitivity the Force-
283	Decks software and their auto-movement identiﬁcation.
284	Frequency of Testing:
285	●	Eccentric utilization ratio (EUR): Since this type of metric isn’t meant to be used for 
286	monitoring purposes, so this would be done before and after training phases in combi-
287	nation with counter movement jump. To calculate EUR: CMJ Jump Ht / SJ Jump Ht
288	Equipment: 
289	●	Contact mat or Force Plates
290	Drop Jump, Reactive Strength Index 
291	Description: The drop jump reactive strength index (DJ-RSI) is mean to assess the stretch 
292	shortening cycle in the lower leg, more speciﬁcally the Fast SSC function which is more asso-
293	ciated with smaller joint angles speciﬁcally around the ankle joint. The suggestion is to provide 
294	an incremental height you drop from so you can derive a “plyometric” proﬁle of the athlete. e.g. 
295	20cm, 30cm, 40cm, 50cm, etc until the athlete has completed a drop jump that resulted in a 
296	lower value than their previous test. Then, for subsequent testing of RSI, you would utilize the 
297	height they derived their best RSI. This may cause issues for teams, but with the number of 
298	contact mats we have available to us, you could arrange 4 diﬀerent heights for 2 mats and that 
299	should cover most teams.
300	How to Test: 
301	●	Stand on box with hands on hips.
302	
303	===== PAGE 15 =====
304	15
305	●	Instruct the athlete to take a small double leg hop oﬀ the box
306	●	Prior to hopping oﬀ the box, instruct the athlete to ensure they jump as high as possi-
307	ble oﬀ the mat while getting oﬀ the mat quickly.
308	●	Instruct the athlete to land with a stiﬀ and stable landing. This is important to gauge 
309	appropriate jump height. If you are concerned with the stiﬀ landing, you can have the 
310	athlete do a small rebound hop after they make contact with the mat upon landing.
311	●	Have athlete perform 3 jumps.
312	Frequency of Testing:
313	●	RSI has been shown to be a valid means of assessing Fast SSC performance. If your 
314	training is prescribed with the desired improvements in Fast SSC function, then you 
315	would perform a pre and post phase assessment. If you are conscious of monitoring 
316	weekly progress or decrement, then during this phase of training, weekly or bi-weekly 
317	testing can be appropriate to help modify workloads.
318	●	 During the competition phases of training, this can be a worthwhile test to be apart of 
319	your monitoring battery since Fast SSC function is sensitive to low-frequency fatigue. 
320	So consider weekly testing during competitions phases of training. If athletes are hesi-
321	tant of performing DJ during the season, then if you have access to the force plate, 
322	RSImod may be a better option.
323	Validity and Reliability:
324	●	There are concerns with reliability with this assessment, especially for non-jumping 
325	athletes, and underdeveloped athletes. So, ensure you go through proper teaching 
326	progressions before utilizing this assessment/monitoring tool.
327	Interpretation of RSI Values:
328	
329	===== PAGE 16 =====
330	16
331	 
332	 
333	Equipment: 
334	●	Contact Mat or Force Plates
335	Weighted Jumps 
336	Description: Weighted jumps oﬀer additional insight with the athletes power and impulse rela-
337	tionship. As power decreases with jumps, impulse will go up until the load is too heavy and 
338	jumping strategy becomes compromised. Since impulse is a function of Force and Time, an in-
339	cremental load and analysis can be utilized to oﬀer a force/velocity relationship in jumping that 
340	may be more speciﬁc than a DSI analysis because of the joint angles associated with the IMTP . 
341	
342	===== PAGE 17 =====
343	17
344	How to Test:
345	●	When performing a F/V jumping proﬁle, you will ﬁrst need to capture a jump height of 
346	CMJ with hands on hips.
347	●	The athlete’s next jump will be done with an empty 15 or 20kg barbell on back.
348	●	You will perform 4-5 jumps that range from 0-80% of the athlete’s body mass.
349	●	When you are ﬁnished, the MyJump app if used will provide you with the information 
350	you require. If you perform this with the use of a Gymaware device, and if the results 
351	are saved in the cloud, you can extract the data and it can be ﬁlled into the Sports Sci-
352	ence excel sheet to give you what MyJump provides. This sheet is not developed 
353	yet, but if this is requested, we will get on this.
354	Frequency of Testing:
355	●	Before and after your training phases to gauge how far oﬀ optimization the athlete is, 
356	and what sort of interventions they further require.
357	Equipment: 
358	●	Gymaware or MyJump (IOS app)
359	
360	
361	===== PAGE 18 =====
362	18
363	Maximal Strength Assessments 
364	1 RM Estimation - Maximal Strength 
365	Description: For maximal strength determination, practitioners are getting away of performing 
366	1RM attempts in the weight room primarily due to the risk associated with it, and the subse-
367	quent cause of undue fatigue that may negatively hinder performance for multiple days after — 
368	especially if there is a large emotional component during the lift. The alternate is velocity based 
369	1RM estimation. This is performed at Iowa with a linear displacement transducer (Gymaware) 
370	attached to the barbell while the athlete performs 1 repetition for multiple loads. Once the ef-
371	forts are completed, the use of linear regression is used to estimate the 1RM.
372	How to Test:
373	●	After the athlete ﬁnished some light weight warm-up repetitions, begin with roughly a 
374	50% load. This load, and all subsequent loads must be done with the same eccentric 
375	tempo with a maximal concentric phase. The repetition average velocity (m/s) and 
376	weight will be recorded.
377	●	Continue taking roughly 10% increments until you reach 85-90% loads, or when the 
378	athlete reaches around 0.1-0.15+ of the associated mean velocity at 1RM below.
379	●	Associated Mean Velocity at 1 RM
380	◦	Squat & Variations: 0.3 m/s
381	◦	Bench & Variations: 0.2 m/s
382	◦	Bench Rows & Variations: 0.5 m/s
383	◦	Power Hang Snatch & Variations: 1 m/s
384	◦	Power Hang Clean & Variations: 0.8 m/s
385	
386	===== PAGE 19 =====
387	19
388	Please be aware of those associated mean velocities at 1RM loads are represen-
389	tative of the average in the populations sampled. Don’t take the velocities as hard 
390	rules, just guidelines 
391	Frequency of Testing:
392	●	Before and after your training phases to gauge how much development has occured.
393	●	If the athlete is performing their lifts with the Gymaware device on every week, you can 
394	gauge a rather accurate representation on how 1RM performance is changing without 
395	waiting until your training phases is done.
396	Equipment: 
397	●	Gymaware
398	Isometric Mid Thigh Pull (IMTP) 
399	Description: The isometric mid thigh pull is a maximal strength test for the lower body. It is de-
400	signed to ensure a reliable measurement of mechanical force production in a joint conﬁgura-
401	tion that is safe, yet gives insight to a number of key variables, such as the rate of force pro-
402	duction and peak force. Additionally, peak isometric force is highly related to maximal strength 
403	in a variety of dynamic lifts and therefore it may be used as a substitute to traditional repetition 
404	maximal testing.
405	How to Test:
406	●	Setup the athlete on the force plate and position them in the position 1 conﬁguration 
407	for the clean. This suggests the torso is upright, weight is through the mid-foot / heel, 
408	feet under hips, and knees are bent at 30-35’. Once the athlete has been coached into 
409	the right position, note the positional number on the IMTP device for subsequent test-
410	ing.
411	●	Ensure the athlete is using straps so grip strength will not limit the lower body force de-
412	velopment.
413	
414	===== PAGE 20 =====
415	20
416	●	Before the test begins, have the athlete go through 2-3 submaximal repetitions before 
417	their maximal repetition.
418	●	When coaching, ensure the athlete is pulling straight up and not pulling backwards.
419	●	To eﬀectively perform the maximal repetition, have the athlete pull 5-10% eﬀort and 
420	then watch the Force Decks software. There should be a stable force application be-
421	fore they pull maximally. You do this to get the slack out of the body and into the right 
422	position so you eliminate jerk. 
423	●	When the athlete has established a stable force application, count them down and 
424	then yell, “PULL!”. Have them hold that maximal contraction for at least 4 seconds.
425	Frequency of Testing:
426	●	Before and after your training phases to gauge how much development has occured.
427	●	Whenever you require a new DSI measurement
428	Interpretation of Results:
429	●	Peak force, and RFD at 50-250ms are of primary concern here. RFD at particular time 
430	frames are always in reference to the athletes peak force. If an athlete produces 3000 
431	newtons of peak force and their RFD at 200ms is 2700 newtons, they have eﬀectively 
432	displayed 90% of their maximal force in 200ms
433	●	Peak force is utilized within the Dynamic Strength Index (DSI).
434	◦	To calculate DSI, you take the CMJ Peak Force / IMTP Peak Force 
435	0.0 - 0.6 = More Ballistic Training, 0.6 - 0.8 = Mixed Program, 0.8-1.0 = More 
436	Maximal Strength Training 
437	Equipment: 
438	●	Force Plates
439	
440	===== PAGE 21 =====
441	21
442	
443	
444	===== PAGE 22 =====
445	22
446	Endurance Assessments 
447	5/1/5 Step Test 
448	Description: The 5/1/5 Step Test is an incremental step test taken to exhaustion. The test uti-
449	lizes a number of sensors to give insight to the oxygen loop (respiratory, transport, utilization). 
450	This is a high level test that provides a lot of valuable insight. This is particularly useful in more 
451	seasoned athletes, or athletes that are simply not progressing with sound prescription. It can 
452	help uncover limitations and provide better “zones” for the athlete. This assessment is only 
453	beneﬁcial for mixed sport positions that require a very large aerobic component, and all en-
454	durance sports besides swimmers.
455	How to Test:
456	●	No warm-up is allowed
457	●	Once the devices are setup on the athlete, they will stand or sit still on the treadmill, 
458	bike, or rower for 1 minute .
459	●	The ﬁrst stage will begin at a low eﬀort pace (e.g. 3.0 mph on a treadmill)
460	●	After 5 minutes of continuous eﬀort, they will cease all activity for 1 minute.
461	●	After the rest period of 1 minute, they will proceed to the next stage with a higher ve-
462	locity or power output.
463	●	This is continued until the athlete is to near exhaustion, RPE 9-10
464	●	The goal is to complete at least 5 stages. 
465	●	For the completion of this assessment, ask Landon to help you run it.
466	Frequency of Testing:
467	
468	===== PAGE 23 =====
469	23
470	●	Before and after your training phases to gauge how much development has occurred 
471	and to reassess their new limitations. 
472	●	In certain sports, this can be done in the competitive period as there can be plenty of 
473	developmental opportunities before their championship portion of their season.
474	Equipment: 
475	●	Treadmill, bike, or rower. Moxy devices (ideally 3), Zephyr or Garmin HR monitor 
476	(Zephyr will provide respiratory frequency (RF)), Pulse oximeter, Peripedal software
477	Yo-Yo Level 1 or 2 Intermittent Test 
478	Description: The yo-yo intermittent recovery test (Yo-Yo IRT) is utilized because it has been 
479	viewed as a valid and reliable estimate of aerobic endurance, is simple and eﬃcient to admin-
480	ister, and has been suﬃciently researched and validated with many diﬀerent sports. 
481	How to Test:
482	●	Measure out 25m on a zero slope pitch/ﬁeld/court
483	●	Place markers at the 0m line, 5m line, and 25m line.
484	●	The 0-5m zone is the walking zone. 5-25m is the running zone
485	●	To start the test, it is best to utilize an audio track that has been designed with the ap-
486	propriate speed tempo, rest, and incremental speed adjustments. You’ll need a smart 
487	phone and speaker for this.
488	●	The athlete continues each stage until they fail to cross the line before the end of the 
489	stage.
490	●	Yo-Yo IRT1 starts at a lower speed and has smaller increments in speed than the Yo-Yo 
491	IRT2.
492	
493	===== PAGE 24 =====
494	24
495	●	Yo-Yo IRT1 is used to determine an athletes individual endurance capacity and may be 
496	more suited to younger athletes. 
497	●	Yo-Yo IRT2 is used to determine the capacity of an athlete to recover from repeated 
498	exercise that requires a high contribution from the anaerobic systems
499	●	If an athlete is able to run faster than speed level 23 on Yo-Yo IRT1, they should per-
500	form the Yo-Yo IRT2 on the next occasion.
501	Frequency of Testing:
502	●	This type of assessment is usually done at the beginning of longer training phases, and 
503	usually is employed before pre-competition phases.
504	Interpretation of Results:
505	●	Test data for a variety of teams from other countries will be provided later, but if you re-
506	quire them before that is ﬁnished, please ask Landon.
507	●	If you want to estimate VO2Max, you can use the test results
508	◦	Yo-Yo IRT1 distance (m) x 0.0084 + 36.4
509	◦	Yo-Yo IRT2 distance (m) x 0.0136 + 45.3
510	Equipment: 
511	●	Cones, audio ﬁle, speaker
512	Repeat Sprint Ability (RSA) 
513	Description: The Repeat Sprint Ability assessment is to gauge the eﬃciency of repeated neuro-
514	muscular eﬀorts. This is particularly useful in sports that have periods of time where their is a 
515	number of high intensity sprinting eﬀorts with a short period of rest between them. This test of-
516	fers two primary elements: To gauge the sprinting time across 20-30 meters, and to gauge the 
517	decrement of performance over subsequent sprint eﬀorts.
518	
519	===== PAGE 25 =====
520	25
521	How to Test:
522	●	After proper warm-up, the athletes are to run 6, 20-30m sprints with 30 seconds of rest 
523	between eﬀorts.
524	●	Times for all sprints are gathered.
525	Frequency of Testing:
526	Interpretation of Results:
527	●	Ideal time(s) = Best time x 6
528	●	Decrement (%) = (Total / Ideal) x 100
529	●	Generally speaking you’re looking for a decrement between 2-10% at most. 
530	●	If greater than 10%, you may consider having the athlete perform more aerobic based 
531	training. If less than 10%, then you may consider having the athlete perform more 
532	speed based training.
533	Equipment: 
534	●	Timing gates or FreeLap
535	
536	
537	===== PAGE 26 =====
538	26
539	Speed Assessments 
540	Linear Sprinting 
541	Description: Linear sprinting with highly sensitive and reliable timing equipment is one of the 
542	most powerful assessment tools that oﬀers insight to the success of the development of your 
543	locomotive athletes. When you perform the test with multiple distances you can eﬀectively 
544	identify where an athlete may need to speed more time in their development.
545	How to Test:
546	●	To ensure a higher reliability, it is suggested for most sport athletes to utilize a 2 point 
547	start.
548	●	For most of your testing with the athletes, you will want the athlete to self select their 
549	start vs being initiated to started on your command.
550	●	Have them run maximally for 30-40 meters.
551	●	Have them perform at least 2 sprints.
552	Frequency of Testing:
553	●	Since most programs have sprinting built into their training, the frequency can be as 
554	frequent as you train. But there is a clear diﬀerence between training and testing, so to 
555	eﬀectively gauge test-to-test improvements, ensure you are not just relying on training 
556	data if you have previous testing data your utilizing.
557	●	If you are not measuring during training, then it is suggested that before and after train-
558	ing phases this is performed. 
559	Interpretation of Results:
560	●	0-10m is considered their acceleration score
561	
562	===== PAGE 27 =====
563	27
564	◦	If you are working more on maximal strength, power, and slow SSC development, 
565	you should predictably see this phase improve.
566	●	30-40m is considered their speed score
567	◦	If you are working more on sprinting, and fast SSC development, you should pre-
568	dictably see this phase improve.
569	●	0-40m is their combined
570	●	40m peak velocity (m/s) - take the 30m split time and subtract it from the 40m split 
571	time and decide by 10 for this value.
572	●	Momentum score (kg x m/s): maximal velocity multiplied by body mass of athlete (kg)
573	Equipment: 
574	●	FreeLap or SmartSpeed
575
