===== PAGE 1 =====
University of Iowa Sports 
Performance Assessment 
Manual 


===== PAGE 2 =====
2
Table of of Contents 
1. Why Assessments 
2. Speciﬁc vs General Tests 
3. Validity & Reliability 
4. Detecting Change 
5. Reassessment 
6. Gender Differences 
7. Team Cultures and Assessments 
8. Iowa Sport Assessment Table 
9. Common Assessments 


===== PAGE 3 =====
3
Why Assessments? 
“The primary aim of testing is to obtain information that assists the coach in creating an in-
dividual plan for each athlete. It is, of course, true that testing an athlete can help to moti-
vate both athlete and practitioner or support the eﬃcacy of a particular training method, 
but these outcomes should be considered secondary to the primary aim of GAINING IN-
FORMATION that informs the practitioner’s training program design.”   
 Jeremy Sheppard and Tim Gabbett  
Speciﬁc Tests vs General Tests 
Sport speciﬁc tests have utility with the assessment process, but rarely is the strength & condi-
tioning coach grading or assessing such processes. Typically, the goal of the strength & condi-
tioning coach is to utilize more general tests that provide the some of the underpinning deter-
minants of such speciﬁc tasks in sports. 
An example is the vertical jump seen in basketball, volleyball, and diving. The vertical jump 
outcomes may be similar across athletes, but the underpinnings of vertical jump relate to im-
pulse (Force x Time). So an athlete would need to examine the maximal force production abili-
ty, and also tasks that require force developed rapidly. IMTP , Back Squat, Deadlift for maximal 
strength, and ballistic exercises such as cleans, snatches, jump squats for explosive strength 
may provide a clearer picture of where an athlete needs to spend time to enhance their vertical 
jump performance.


===== PAGE 4 =====
4
Validity 
A valid test measures what it is intended to measure (and is considered suﬃciently reliable to 
use).
Types of Validity 
●	Ecological: refers to how well the assessment tool relates to actual athlete perfor-
mance and how well the ﬁndings can be applied in real-life settings.
●	Construct: refers to the overall validity, or the extend to which the test actually mea-
sures what it is designed to measure.
●	Face: is the appearance to the athlete, coach, and other practitioners that the test 
measures what it is purported to measure.
●	Content: refers to the expert assessment that the monitoring tool measures what it 
claims to measure.
●	Criterion: refers to the relationship between the scores on the test and scores on a cri-
terion measure. Criterion measure is a test that is widely accepted as a gold-standard 
and valid test. E.g. Force plates for force testing vs deriving force from a displacement 
sensor (e.g. Gymaware).
●	Concurrent: refers to the validity of a test for measuring a construct at a particular 
time. In most cases, the test is correlated with another, more accurate measure of the 
construct that is not feasible in most sport situations (e.g. Doing a 3km time trail on the 
day of competition)
●	Predictive: refers to the ability of a test to predict some construct or outcome in the 
future.

===== PAGE 5 =====
5
Reliability 
The reliability of a measure (test) can be viewed simply as the amount of variation that occurs 
from one test occasion to another.
Learning eﬀect: Athletes should have at least 3-4 familiarization trials to reduce any learning 
eﬀects. For instance, before performing an isometric-mid-thigh-pull (IMTP) assessment, the 
athlete(s) should get accustomed to the position of pulling, the use of straps, and sensation 
prior to the real assessment. If you're ﬁnding yourself having to coach the task quite a bit, the 
athlete will likely experience improvements the next time they assess simply by the learning ef-
fect.
Types of Reliability 
1.	Interrater reliability: refers to the degree to which diﬀerent people conducting the as-
sessment agree in their test results over time or on repeated occasions.
2.	Intrarater reliability: refers to the consistency of scores in repeated tests conducted by 
a single tester.
Detecting Change 
The sensitivity of a assessment (or even a monitoring) tool refers to its ability to detect small 
but important changes in performance or an aspect such as fatigue. 
Meaningful change is deﬁned as the smallest practical change that is important. 
To ensure meaningful change is occurring, please allow the Sports Science depart-
ment to help provide you (the S&C coach) insight into this area as this is beyond this 
manual at this time. 


===== PAGE 6 =====
6
Reassessment 
Reassessment is primarily dependent upon three factors:
●	Time within the competition year. There is a contextual evaluation that must occur to 
ensure proper placement of assessments. This is especially more important the closer 
one is to the competition period.
●	The expectation of change. If you are in a maximal strength phase  for a beginner or in-
termediate athlete, you may consider reassessing in 4 weeks. If the athlete is and ad-
vanced athlete, you may consider a longer period. This is also dependent upon the 
length of the phase. The length of training period would extend the reassessment date 
to allow for adequate recovery to occur.
●	Unexpected recovery issues. Do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue. A big 
reason for reassessment is to provide the athlete the conﬁdence they are improving. 
Ensure their readiness matches their assessment needs. This may require multiple as-
sessment dates for a team sport, or a larger group of individuals. Be ﬂexible.
Gender Differences 
The primary consideration here is the female menstrual cycle. To complicate matters more, if a 
female is utilizing birth control, there are a  number of variables that are diﬃcult to control for. 
In general, the two primary phases of the menstrual cycle that a practitioner should be aware 
of is the follicular and the luteal phase. 
The follicular phase is the ﬁrst phase of the menstrual cycle. This phase has the association of 
an increase of testosterone and estrogen. In terms of adaptability of training stressors, women 
that perform more strength/power/speed based work during this phase may adapt better. This 
may also be the same for the assessment of strength/power/speed.
The luteal phase is the second phase of the menstrual cycle. This phase has the association 
with a decrease of testosterone, estrogen, and the increase of progesterone. In terms of adapt-
===== PAGE 7 =====
7
ability of training stressors, women's that perform more endurance based work during this 
phase may adapt better. This may also be the same for the assessment of endurance.
Considerations and reality. 
Ideally, you and the medical staﬀ are aware of your female student-athletes menstrual cycle 
history, length, and even medications. This may help aide in training design and assessment 
procedures. 
In reality, most will not have access to this. And even though if available, in team sports, this 
may never enter into the decision making processes. 
 In summary, team communication and transparency, monitoring procedures, 
relationships, and general sound heuristics should drive your decision making. If you feel 
an athlete's readiness is not going to match the requirements for assessment then 
consider postponing. 
Team Cultures and Assessments 
There will be a number of speciﬁc and even general assessments that you may likely never do 
because they are already happening within sport practice already. This doesn’t necessarily 
mean you dismiss the assessments, but you can use their information to help triangulate what 
you’re seeing to come up with possible valuable insight to the athlete and coaching staﬀ. Addi-
tionally, in regards to meaningful change, this is where you can employ help from the Sports 
Science staﬀ to help give your coaching staﬀ(s) more conﬁdence there was actual change that 
they can be conﬁdent with.


===== PAGE 8 =====
8
Athlete Preparation Before Testing 
The preparation instructions ensure two things
●	The student-athlete is in the best possible condition prior to their assessment(s)
●	To ensure test to test reliability
Instructions: 
●	Diet: 
◦	Athletes should be encourage to consume a series of high-carbohydrate meals in 
the 36 hours prior to testing and arrive on test day well hydrated.
◦	No food or caﬀeine are to be consumed in the 2 hours prior to testing
●	Training: 
◦	No training inducing severe physiological or neural fatigue should be undertaken in 
48-72 hours prior to testing. This includes any high-intensity skill training as well.
●	Testing:
◦	All test sessions should be scheduled at the same time of day (ideally) to avoid 
ﬂuctuations in physioloigcal response to set procotrols due to circadian rhythm. All 
tests must be completed in the recommended standarized order with adequate 
and consistent recovery tiem between tests. This will promote optimal perfor-
mance and allow for valid comparison of results on diﬀerent test occasions.


===== PAGE 9 =====
9
Iowa Sport Assessment Table 
 
 


===== PAGE 10 =====
10
General Assessments 
Physical Competency Assessment (PCA) 
Description: The Physical Competency Assessment is a S&C developed global assessment to 
give fundamental information regarding the preparedness to train. Preparedness to compete is 
not being assessed here. This assessment will always be done with a battery of physical based 
assessments (e.g. mechanical power testing) and non-physical assessments (e.g. TMG, Ome-
gawave).
Frequency of Testing: There should be a minimal of ONE time per year where this assessment 
should be performed. The most impactful time(s) is when your student-athletes have been 
away from campus for an extended period of time and/or after the competition season.
Consider retesting "at risk" exercises more frequently if you are actively working to-
wards modifying the risk (e.g. Large single leg squat deﬁcit) 
Validity & Reliability: This assessment has been formulated by the Strength & Conditioning 
department. In general, we are not aware of the reliability and validity of the assessment. But 
general heuristics would tell us it is a means to an end, and helps foster unknown intelligence 
regarding a student-athlete by not necessarily the tests themselves, but with the conversations 
that follow.
Anthropometrics 
Description: Anthropometrics have a strong association with success for most sports. There 
are certain heights, weights, limb lengths, and muscle/fat ratios that appear to help optimize 
performance outcomes. 
Frequency of Testing: 
●	Height: 1x
●	Limb lengths: 1x

===== PAGE 11 =====
11
●	Bodyweight: Weekly
●	Body composition (if available via scanning/measuring): No more than 4x / year
●	Body composition (skin fold sums): BI-monthly or monthly
Validity & Reliability: The assessment of height, limb lengths, and bodyweight are valid and 
reliable. The scales that we utilized at Iowa are tested around 2x per year. Body composition is 
a valid tool, but the typical error in the “best” devices can still be as low as +/-4%. Meaning, if 
you your body composition and review the body fat % value and its 15%, the actual range you 
would fall between 11-19%. So if the athlete changes their behaviors to induce a body fat drop 
and they re-test, and it says 15% again, can you be certain they didn’t get any leaner? No, be-
cause they could have gotten leaner (perhaps you can visually see, their bodyweight has 
dropped), but they were simply a victim of typical error which is a function of technology vari-
ation and biological variation. So, you need to utilize other information to best deliver your 
analysis.


===== PAGE 12 =====
12
Jump Assessments 
Counter Movement Jump 
Description: The counter movement jump (CMJ) oﬀers a lot of insight about the athletes per-
formance abilities by itself, when used in combination with other tests, and is a useful tool to 
gauge compensatory patterns (when using the force plate), and can be a valid tool to monitor 
neuromuscular fatigue.
How to Test:
●	Stand on the jump mat or force plate with hands on hips. 
●	Instruct the athlete to simply jump as high as possible. Do not coach strategy of jump-
ing.
●	Instruct the athlete to land with a stiﬀ and stable landing. This is important to gauge 
appropriate jump height and also peak landing force when on the force plate.
●	 Have athlete perform 3 jumps.
Frequency of testing:
●	Asymmetry analysis: 1x / month, unless athlete has rich injury history or is coming 
back from an injury
●	Peak concentric force (for Dynamic Strength Index (DSI)): Whenever you feel there is a 
need to ﬁnd their new DSI to make appropriate interventional changes. During the oﬀ-
season, this is appropriate before and after each training phase. Suggestion Utilize 
DSI more frequently with your more developed athletes as most underdeveloped ath-
letes simply need a good mixed program, and likely one that favors strength develop-
ment over other forms of training (e.g. speed, power)
●	Jump Height: Weekly or Before and after training phases. Depends on your purpose. If 
you are going weekly, you will want to utilize the AVERAGE jump height across 3 
===== PAGE 13 =====
13
jumps. This appears to be a valid form of neuromuscular fatigue monitoring. If you are 
testing before and after training phases, and jump height is a key performance indica-
tor (e.g. basketball, volleyball, diving), then you should gauge the improvement of this if 
that is being targeted. For instance, after a maximal strength phase with a more devel-
oped athlete, jump height may go down as there still is residual fatigue. In a lesser de-
veloped athlete, it may go up after any form of training. So it is critical to contextual 
frame the outcomes for your athletes.
Jump height when using it for monitoring (average of 3 jumps), KPI monitoring, 
or it’s inclusion into the Eccentric Utilization Ratio (EUR) analysis can be all done 
on the contact mat. 
●	 RSImod: Weekly, especially during in-season or phases of training where you feel the 
speed and technical demand is high. Since RSImod is an eﬃciency metric, it can pro-
vide you insight of the jump strategy in relation to the ﬂight time. This output is provid-
ed via the ForceDecks software. 
Equipment:
●	Contact Mat (only for Jump Height), Force Plate (Asymmetry, Jump Height, Peak Con-
centric Force, RSImod)
 Squat Jump 
Description: The squat jump (SJ) is similar to the CMJ, but minus the eccentric (or lowering) 
phase of the CMJ. This is to help determine the athlete’s ability to utilize their stretch shorten-
ing cycle (SSC) in the jumping pattern, more specially the Slow SSC function which is more as-
sociated with larger joint angles specially around the knee and hip joints.
How to Test:
●	Stand on the jump mat or force plate with hands on hips. 
●	Instruct the athlete to lower down into the bottom of their CMJ position and pause in 
that position for 3-4 seconds. This time is necessary to remove much of the SSC con-
centric contribution.

===== PAGE 14 =====
14
●	Upon command, Instruct the athlete to simply jump as high as possible without dip-
ping down.
●	Instruct the athlete to land with a stiﬀ and stable landing. This is important to gauge 
appropriate jump height and also peak landing force when on the force plate.
●	 Have athlete perform 3 jumps.
●	This test is more suitable on the contact mat because of the high sensitivity the Force-
Decks software and their auto-movement identiﬁcation.
Frequency of Testing:
●	Eccentric utilization ratio (EUR): Since this type of metric isn’t meant to be used for 
monitoring purposes, so this would be done before and after training phases in combi-
nation with counter movement jump. To calculate EUR: CMJ Jump Ht / SJ Jump Ht
Equipment: 
●	Contact mat or Force Plates
Drop Jump, Reactive Strength Index 
Description: The drop jump reactive strength index (DJ-RSI) is mean to assess the stretch 
shortening cycle in the lower leg, more speciﬁcally the Fast SSC function which is more asso-
ciated with smaller joint angles speciﬁcally around the ankle joint. The suggestion is to provide 
an incremental height you drop from so you can derive a “plyometric” proﬁle of the athlete. e.g. 
20cm, 30cm, 40cm, 50cm, etc until the athlete has completed a drop jump that resulted in a 
lower value than their previous test. Then, for subsequent testing of RSI, you would utilize the 
height they derived their best RSI. This may cause issues for teams, but with the number of 
contact mats we have available to us, you could arrange 4 diﬀerent heights for 2 mats and that 
should cover most teams.
How to Test: 
●	Stand on box with hands on hips.

===== PAGE 15 =====
15
●	Instruct the athlete to take a small double leg hop oﬀ the box
●	Prior to hopping oﬀ the box, instruct the athlete to ensure they jump as high as possi-
ble oﬀ the mat while getting oﬀ the mat quickly.
●	Instruct the athlete to land with a stiﬀ and stable landing. This is important to gauge 
appropriate jump height. If you are concerned with the stiﬀ landing, you can have the 
athlete do a small rebound hop after they make contact with the mat upon landing.
●	Have athlete perform 3 jumps.
Frequency of Testing:
●	RSI has been shown to be a valid means of assessing Fast SSC performance. If your 
training is prescribed with the desired improvements in Fast SSC function, then you 
would perform a pre and post phase assessment. If you are conscious of monitoring 
weekly progress or decrement, then during this phase of training, weekly or bi-weekly 
testing can be appropriate to help modify workloads.
●	 During the competition phases of training, this can be a worthwhile test to be apart of 
your monitoring battery since Fast SSC function is sensitive to low-frequency fatigue. 
So consider weekly testing during competitions phases of training. If athletes are hesi-
tant of performing DJ during the season, then if you have access to the force plate, 
RSImod may be a better option.
Validity and Reliability:
●	There are concerns with reliability with this assessment, especially for non-jumping 
athletes, and underdeveloped athletes. So, ensure you go through proper teaching 
progressions before utilizing this assessment/monitoring tool.
Interpretation of RSI Values:

===== PAGE 16 =====
16
 
 
Equipment: 
●	Contact Mat or Force Plates
Weighted Jumps 
Description: Weighted jumps oﬀer additional insight with the athletes power and impulse rela-
tionship. As power decreases with jumps, impulse will go up until the load is too heavy and 
jumping strategy becomes compromised. Since impulse is a function of Force and Time, an in-
cremental load and analysis can be utilized to oﬀer a force/velocity relationship in jumping that 
may be more speciﬁc than a DSI analysis because of the joint angles associated with the IMTP . 

===== PAGE 17 =====
17
How to Test:
●	When performing a F/V jumping proﬁle, you will ﬁrst need to capture a jump height of 
CMJ with hands on hips.
●	The athlete’s next jump will be done with an empty 15 or 20kg barbell on back.
●	You will perform 4-5 jumps that range from 0-80% of the athlete’s body mass.
●	When you are ﬁnished, the MyJump app if used will provide you with the information 
you require. If you perform this with the use of a Gymaware device, and if the results 
are saved in the cloud, you can extract the data and it can be ﬁlled into the Sports Sci-
ence excel sheet to give you what MyJump provides. This sheet is not developed 
yet, but if this is requested, we will get on this.
Frequency of Testing:
●	Before and after your training phases to gauge how far oﬀ optimization the athlete is, 
and what sort of interventions they further require.
Equipment: 
●	Gymaware or MyJump (IOS app)


===== PAGE 18 =====
18
Maximal Strength Assessments 
1 RM Estimation - Maximal Strength 
Description: For maximal strength determination, practitioners are getting away of performing 
1RM attempts in the weight room primarily due to the risk associated with it, and the subse-
quent cause of undue fatigue that may negatively hinder performance for multiple days after — 
especially if there is a large emotional component during the lift. The alternate is velocity based 
1RM estimation. This is performed at Iowa with a linear displacement transducer (Gymaware) 
attached to the barbell while the athlete performs 1 repetition for multiple loads. Once the ef-
forts are completed, the use of linear regression is used to estimate the 1RM.
How to Test:
●	After the athlete ﬁnished some light weight warm-up repetitions, begin with roughly a 
50% load. This load, and all subsequent loads must be done with the same eccentric 
tempo with a maximal concentric phase. The repetition average velocity (m/s) and 
weight will be recorded.
●	Continue taking roughly 10% increments until you reach 85-90% loads, or when the 
athlete reaches around 0.1-0.15+ of the associated mean velocity at 1RM below.
●	Associated Mean Velocity at 1 RM
◦	Squat & Variations: 0.3 m/s
◦	Bench & Variations: 0.2 m/s
◦	Bench Rows & Variations: 0.5 m/s
◦	Power Hang Snatch & Variations: 1 m/s
◦	Power Hang Clean & Variations: 0.8 m/s

===== PAGE 19 =====
19
Please be aware of those associated mean velocities at 1RM loads are represen-
tative of the average in the populations sampled. Don’t take the velocities as hard 
rules, just guidelines 
Frequency of Testing:
●	Before and after your training phases to gauge how much development has occured.
●	If the athlete is performing their lifts with the Gymaware device on every week, you can 
gauge a rather accurate representation on how 1RM performance is changing without 
waiting until your training phases is done.
Equipment: 
●	Gymaware
Isometric Mid Thigh Pull (IMTP) 
Description: The isometric mid thigh pull is a maximal strength test for the lower body. It is de-
signed to ensure a reliable measurement of mechanical force production in a joint conﬁgura-
tion that is safe, yet gives insight to a number of key variables, such as the rate of force pro-
duction and peak force. Additionally, peak isometric force is highly related to maximal strength 
in a variety of dynamic lifts and therefore it may be used as a substitute to traditional repetition 
maximal testing.
How to Test:
●	Setup the athlete on the force plate and position them in the position 1 conﬁguration 
for the clean. This suggests the torso is upright, weight is through the mid-foot / heel, 
feet under hips, and knees are bent at 30-35’. Once the athlete has been coached into 
the right position, note the positional number on the IMTP device for subsequent test-
ing.
●	Ensure the athlete is using straps so grip strength will not limit the lower body force de-
velopment.

===== PAGE 20 =====
20
●	Before the test begins, have the athlete go through 2-3 submaximal repetitions before 
their maximal repetition.
●	When coaching, ensure the athlete is pulling straight up and not pulling backwards.
●	To eﬀectively perform the maximal repetition, have the athlete pull 5-10% eﬀort and 
then watch the Force Decks software. There should be a stable force application be-
fore they pull maximally. You do this to get the slack out of the body and into the right 
position so you eliminate jerk. 
●	When the athlete has established a stable force application, count them down and 
then yell, “PULL!”. Have them hold that maximal contraction for at least 4 seconds.
Frequency of Testing:
●	Before and after your training phases to gauge how much development has occured.
●	Whenever you require a new DSI measurement
Interpretation of Results:
●	Peak force, and RFD at 50-250ms are of primary concern here. RFD at particular time 
frames are always in reference to the athletes peak force. If an athlete produces 3000 
newtons of peak force and their RFD at 200ms is 2700 newtons, they have eﬀectively 
displayed 90% of their maximal force in 200ms
●	Peak force is utilized within the Dynamic Strength Index (DSI).
◦	To calculate DSI, you take the CMJ Peak Force / IMTP Peak Force 
0.0 - 0.6 = More Ballistic Training, 0.6 - 0.8 = Mixed Program, 0.8-1.0 = More 
Maximal Strength Training 
Equipment: 
●	Force Plates

===== PAGE 21 =====
21


===== PAGE 22 =====
22
Endurance Assessments 
5/1/5 Step Test 
Description: The 5/1/5 Step Test is an incremental step test taken to exhaustion. The test uti-
lizes a number of sensors to give insight to the oxygen loop (respiratory, transport, utilization). 
This is a high level test that provides a lot of valuable insight. This is particularly useful in more 
seasoned athletes, or athletes that are simply not progressing with sound prescription. It can 
help uncover limitations and provide better “zones” for the athlete. This assessment is only 
beneﬁcial for mixed sport positions that require a very large aerobic component, and all en-
durance sports besides swimmers.
How to Test:
●	No warm-up is allowed
●	Once the devices are setup on the athlete, they will stand or sit still on the treadmill, 
bike, or rower for 1 minute .
●	The ﬁrst stage will begin at a low eﬀort pace (e.g. 3.0 mph on a treadmill)
●	After 5 minutes of continuous eﬀort, they will cease all activity for 1 minute.
●	After the rest period of 1 minute, they will proceed to the next stage with a higher ve-
locity or power output.
●	This is continued until the athlete is to near exhaustion, RPE 9-10
●	The goal is to complete at least 5 stages. 
●	For the completion of this assessment, ask Landon to help you run it.
Frequency of Testing:

===== PAGE 23 =====
23
●	Before and after your training phases to gauge how much development has occurred 
and to reassess their new limitations. 
●	In certain sports, this can be done in the competitive period as there can be plenty of 
developmental opportunities before their championship portion of their season.
Equipment: 
●	Treadmill, bike, or rower. Moxy devices (ideally 3), Zephyr or Garmin HR monitor 
(Zephyr will provide respiratory frequency (RF)), Pulse oximeter, Peripedal software
Yo-Yo Level 1 or 2 Intermittent Test 
Description: The yo-yo intermittent recovery test (Yo-Yo IRT) is utilized because it has been 
viewed as a valid and reliable estimate of aerobic endurance, is simple and eﬃcient to admin-
ister, and has been suﬃciently researched and validated with many diﬀerent sports. 
How to Test:
●	Measure out 25m on a zero slope pitch/ﬁeld/court
●	Place markers at the 0m line, 5m line, and 25m line.
●	The 0-5m zone is the walking zone. 5-25m is the running zone
●	To start the test, it is best to utilize an audio track that has been designed with the ap-
propriate speed tempo, rest, and incremental speed adjustments. You’ll need a smart 
phone and speaker for this.
●	The athlete continues each stage until they fail to cross the line before the end of the 
stage.
●	Yo-Yo IRT1 starts at a lower speed and has smaller increments in speed than the Yo-Yo 
IRT2.

===== PAGE 24 =====
24
●	Yo-Yo IRT1 is used to determine an athletes individual endurance capacity and may be 
more suited to younger athletes. 
●	Yo-Yo IRT2 is used to determine the capacity of an athlete to recover from repeated 
exercise that requires a high contribution from the anaerobic systems
●	If an athlete is able to run faster than speed level 23 on Yo-Yo IRT1, they should per-
form the Yo-Yo IRT2 on the next occasion.
Frequency of Testing:
●	This type of assessment is usually done at the beginning of longer training phases, and 
usually is employed before pre-competition phases.
Interpretation of Results:
●	Test data for a variety of teams from other countries will be provided later, but if you re-
quire them before that is ﬁnished, please ask Landon.
●	If you want to estimate VO2Max, you can use the test results
◦	Yo-Yo IRT1 distance (m) x 0.0084 + 36.4
◦	Yo-Yo IRT2 distance (m) x 0.0136 + 45.3
Equipment: 
●	Cones, audio ﬁle, speaker
Repeat Sprint Ability (RSA) 
Description: The Repeat Sprint Ability assessment is to gauge the eﬃciency of repeated neuro-
muscular eﬀorts. This is particularly useful in sports that have periods of time where their is a 
number of high intensity sprinting eﬀorts with a short period of rest between them. This test of-
fers two primary elements: To gauge the sprinting time across 20-30 meters, and to gauge the 
decrement of performance over subsequent sprint eﬀorts.

===== PAGE 25 =====
25
How to Test:
●	After proper warm-up, the athletes are to run 6, 20-30m sprints with 30 seconds of rest 
between eﬀorts.
●	Times for all sprints are gathered.
Frequency of Testing:
Interpretation of Results:
●	Ideal time(s) = Best time x 6
●	Decrement (%) = (Total / Ideal) x 100
●	Generally speaking you’re looking for a decrement between 2-10% at most. 
●	If greater than 10%, you may consider having the athlete perform more aerobic based 
training. If less than 10%, then you may consider having the athlete perform more 
speed based training.
Equipment: 
●	Timing gates or FreeLap


===== PAGE 26 =====
26
Speed Assessments 
Linear Sprinting 
Description: Linear sprinting with highly sensitive and reliable timing equipment is one of the 
most powerful assessment tools that oﬀers insight to the success of the development of your 
locomotive athletes. When you perform the test with multiple distances you can eﬀectively 
identify where an athlete may need to speed more time in their development.
How to Test:
●	To ensure a higher reliability, it is suggested for most sport athletes to utilize a 2 point 
start.
●	For most of your testing with the athletes, you will want the athlete to self select their 
start vs being initiated to started on your command.
●	Have them run maximally for 30-40 meters.
●	Have them perform at least 2 sprints.
Frequency of Testing:
●	Since most programs have sprinting built into their training, the frequency can be as 
frequent as you train. But there is a clear diﬀerence between training and testing, so to 
eﬀectively gauge test-to-test improvements, ensure you are not just relying on training 
data if you have previous testing data your utilizing.
●	If you are not measuring during training, then it is suggested that before and after train-
ing phases this is performed. 
Interpretation of Results:
●	0-10m is considered their acceleration score

===== PAGE 27 =====
27
◦	If you are working more on maximal strength, power, and slow SSC development, 
you should predictably see this phase improve.
●	30-40m is considered their speed score
◦	If you are working more on sprinting, and fast SSC development, you should pre-
dictably see this phase improve.
●	0-40m is their combined
●	40m peak velocity (m/s) - take the 30m split time and subtract it from the 40m split 
time and decide by 10 for this value.
●	Momentum score (kg x m/s): maximal velocity multiplied by body mass of athlete (kg)
Equipment: 
●	FreeLap or SmartSpeed

1	BAYLOR ATHLETICS
2	APPLIED PERFORMANCE OPERATIONS GUIDE
3	## [Heading 1] PREPARING CHAMPIONS FOR LIFE
4	INTRODUCTION
5	Participating in 19 varsity sports, Baylor student-athletes compete at the highest level on the field, on the court, and in the classroom, consistently ranking among the Big 12’s and nation’s best. Baylor Athletics stands in support of the university’s important mission to educate men and women for worldwide leadership and service by integrating academic excellence and Christian commitment within a caring community. This mission informs our day-to-day efforts through one simple purpose: PREPARE CHAMPIONS FOR LIFE.
6	DEFINING CHAMPIONS
7	In the context of athletics, the word “champion” evokes images of a game-winning shot, a feat of physical strength, or a trophy hoisted high by a victorious team; but it has much deeper roots. One of the earliest definitions is as “one who fights on behalf of others” (circa 1300), and later “to fight for, defend, or protect” (circa 1820).
8	When we say we will “Prepare Champions for Life,” we are calling to that deeper sense of the word. Each year, more than 500 student-athletes are on campus representing the GREEN and GOLD. Our job is to educate and prepare these individuals in all aspects of their life, so they leave Waco with a depth of understanding of what transforms an individual into a champion.
9	No team or individual is successful without a successful process – a championship process. Baylor Athletics focuses on four key areas of development to ensure our student-athletes receive the training and support we are uniquely equipped to provide.
10	Our championship process rests on these four pillars:
11	ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT
12	ATHLETIC SUCCESS
13	SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
14	SPIRITUAL GROWTH
15	## [Heading 1] ONE STANDARD. ONE ACCORD.
16	Baylor Athletics’ ability to carry out the vision of Preparing Champions for Life hinges on a collective commitment to live by ONE STANDARD – to faithfully steward the authentic pursuit of competitive excellence through Christ. In upholding this standard, the department has committed to be in ONE ACCORD on six scripturally based operating principles and 18 associated core values.
17	We will do our serviceable and personal best. – Ecclesiastes 9:10
18	Purpose | Perseverance | Preeminence
19	We will commit to principled innovation. – Romans 12:2
20	Reflection | Aspiration | Advancement
21	We will master fundamentals and pursue excellence. – Ephesians 2:10
22	Intent | Equip | Championships
23	We will treat one another with dignity and respect. – Colossians 3:12-14
24	Service | Love | Truth
25	We will welcome vulnerability and accountability. – Psalm 139:23-24
26	Inclusivity | Humility | Trust
27	We will make all decisions in accordance with governing regulations. – Galatians 6:9
28	Virtue | Transparent | Vigilance
29	## [Heading 1] HEALTH & WELLNESS
30	ATHLETICS PERFORMANCE
31	The mission of Baylor University Athletics Performance is to set the standard for elite preparation, which will serve as a bridge to life-long student-athlete success while achieving competitive excellence.
32	ATHLETIC MEDICINE
33	Baylor University Athletic Medicine (BUAM) promotes health and safety in sport while maintaining an environment focusing on the Christian mission of Baylor University. BUAM’s objective is to serve the healthcare needs of Baylor student-athletes promptly and precisely to allow them the opportunity to achieve success in athletics and life.
34	PERFORMANCE NUTRITION
35	Baylor Performance Nutrition guides the practical execution of evidence-based nutrition strategies to optimize athletic performance and foster lifelong healthy behaviors. The department provides individual consultations, hosts team education sessions, evaluates and informs student-athletes about supplements, performs body composition and bone density assessments, and oversees the student-athlete training table (Beauchamp Athletics Nutrition Center) and fueling stations.
36	MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES
37	Baylor Athletics Mental Health Services (AMHS) is dedicated to the growth and development of student-athletes through providing the highest quality mental health care. Mental health professionals are available to meet with student-athletes to help them deal with a wide variety of issues that may arise during their collegiate experience. Professional counselors are trained to help student-athletes identify and change ways of thinking or behaving that are potentially contributing to their distress or impairing their functioning. AMHS empowers Baylor student-athletes to discuss their personal concerns in a confidential and nonjudgmental setting.
38	## [Heading 1] APPLIED PERFORMANCE
39	MISSION
40	Operating within the Baylor Athletics Health and Wellness Department, BAYLOR APPLIED PERFORMANCE drives the elite performance of championship-level athletic programs by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships. In fulfilling this mission, Applied Performance aims to enable the high-performance team (Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, Mental Health Services, and sport coaching staffs) to answer team- and/or technology-specific questions, ask better questions based on presented evidence; and discover new questions.
41	OPERATING PRINCIPLES
42	Athlete Monitoring and analysis
43	Use various objective and subjective measures related to health and performance across each season phase (pre-season, in-season, post-season, and off-season).
44	Provide information that supports the Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine staff to determine appropriate training and return-to-performance (RTP) periodization with reference to typical training and competition demands.
45	Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance
46	Identify sport- and position-specific key performance indicators (KPIs).
47	Conduct athlete evaluations for diagnostic screening, performance testing, and KPI threshold identification.
48	Performance Team Collaboration
49	Bring together all members of the high-performance team through effective knowledge dissemination.
50	Provide data to inform the decision-making process throughout Health and Wellness.
51	Research and Development
52	In collaboration with on-campus faculty, conduct internal and external research on the latest performance technologies and trends within intercollegiate athletics.
53	Provide the high-performance team with knowledge to implement best practices for improving student-athlete performance and minimizing injury risk.

466	Other
467	IMA
468	Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) is a set of metrics that measures athlete micro movements and direction regardless of unit orientation. Athlete movements can be quantified into low, medium and high intensity athlete movements zones that are used to construct profiles of athletes’ movements and to recognize biomechanical red flags.
469	IMA gives indoor and outdoor sports the ability to track acceleration count, deceleration count, asymmetrical loading, change of direction (COD) count – left and right, free running event count, free running total time, average stride rate, impacts, and jump count.
470	IMA allows the end user to collect and analyze acceleration- and deceleration-based data without the use of a GPS system. It is beneficial for indoor sessions in which a user cannot collect GPS data. It is also beneficial for breaking down movements into micro movements which can further be analyzed for performance insights.
471	3D Position
472	Perch uses a 3D camera to directly measure the position of objects in the field of view of the camera. Every image that the Perch camera captures contains information about how far away objects are from the camera itself.
473	Using a complex tracking pipeline developed by engineers at Perch, the camera processes the image to find the objects we’re interested in (namely, a barbell, parts of the body, etc.). Once the object is located in the image, the device will use the distance data from the 3D camera and some geometry to triangulate where the object is in 3D space. Otherwise known as determining the 3D coordinate of the object for this particular point in time.
474	3D position, as its name suggests, consists of three spatial dimensions. The names we use for these dimensions are X, Y, and Z. We define Z as up and down (parallel to gravity), X as forwards and backwards (in the perspective of the athlete), and Y as side to side (in the perspective of the athlete).
475	3D Path
476	The 3D path of an object – in our case, usually a barbell – is nothing more than a sequence of 3D coordinates with time stamps. By processing images rapidly as the 3D camera captures them, we collect many 3D coordinates and collect them together to form a 3D path.
477	The 3D path represents precisely where in 3D space an object moved over time. This is the core data that Perch captures, and every other metric is calculated using this 3D path.
478	Displacement
479	Displacement is simply calculated by subtracting a starting 3D position and from an ending position. If you isolate only one of the axes, for example the Z axis, you then have the vertical displacement between those positions. For example, in the case of a back squat, the displacement on the Z axis can be interpreted as the squat depth.
480	Velocity
481	The equation for velocity is always the same: displacement (aka. distance) divided by time. Since we are able to go from 3D position to 3D Path and finally calculate displacement, we’re halfway there. Every 3D coordinate also has a corresponding time associated with it, and we can subtract the times starting and ending 3D coordinates to calculate the amount of time elapsed between those two positions.
482	By dividing the displacement by the time that elapsed between them, you are calculating velocity.
483	Mean Velocity
484	Mean velocity (or average velocity) as used in VBT is defined as the average velocity of a complete movement (e.g. the concentric portion of a rep).
485	Calculating mean velocity is exactly the same as calculating any other velocity, except the start and end 3D positions you choose are the beginning and end of the movement respectively.
486	For example, to calculate the concentric mean velocity (on the Z axis) of a rep, we perform three calculations:
487	We subtract the Z value of the coordinate of the bottom of the rep (the beginning of the concentric movement) from the highest point at the end of the rep (the final coordinate of the concentric movement) to calculate the displacement.
488	We subtract the times of the same two coordinates chosen above to calculate the duration of the concentric movement.
489	Finally, we divide the displacement by the duration to get the velocity.
490	Concentric and Eccentric Mean Velocity are both captured in the system and are registered separately – one will not impact the other.
491	Peak Velocity
492	Calculating peak velocity is once again very similar to other velocity calculations, however it differs in selection of the coordinates.
493	Peak velocity is defined as the greatest instantaneous velocity during a movement. Here, “instantaneous” means between two consecutive coordinates. Naturally, there is some amount of time between each coordinate we measure, so using two adjacent coordinates is not truly instantaneous, but is sufficiently close.
494	As an example, to find the peak concentric velocity (on the Z axis), we do the following:
495	Compute the instantaneous velocity using every pair of consecutive coordinates from the lowest to the highest point of the movement (following the same procedure as defined above)
496	The largest of these instantaneous velocities is your peak concentric velocity
497	Eccentric Time
498	Eccentric time is tracking the amount of time, in seconds, it takes to complete the eccentric portion of the movement. This is not displayed on the tablet for Olympic lifts or for jumps.
499	We subtract the Z value of the coordinate of the top of the rep (the beginning of the eccentric movement) from the lowest point at the end of the rep (the final coordinate of the eccentric movement). We subtract the times of the same two coordinates to calculate the duration of the eccentric movement.
500	Power
501	The equation for power is defined as Work divided by time: P = W / t
502	In our case, the force is how much force the athlete is applying to the barbell. While we’ve already covered how we can calculate velocity (the Vterm), we can’t directly measure the force. However, we can calculate it in a couple different ways depending on the context.
503	Mean Power
504	Mean power can be described as the average amount of power over the duration of the movement. To calculate, we can reuse the mean velocity we’ve already calculated above for the V term in our power equations.
505	The force (F) in our equation is similarly the average force applied by the athlete during the movement. Because the bar is at rest before and after the movement, the average force is equal to the force required to oppose gravity (aka, the force of gravity) on the barbell. As such, the force is the mass of the barbell (in kilograms) multiplied by the acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/s).
506	With the math established, calculating mean power is as simple as substituting the mass of the barbell (converted to kilograms, m) and the mean velocity (in meters per second, V) into the following equation: Mean Power = m x 9.8 x V
507	Peak Power
508	Calculating peak power requires a bit more complexity, as was the case with peak velocity.
509	In order to calculate the peak power output for a movement, we calculate the instantaneous power at every point during the movement and select the largest.
510	Here is the general procedure for how we calculate peak power for a concentric movement:
511	Using the same procedure as in peak velocity, calculate the instantaneous velocity for every pair of points in the movement.
512	Using every consecutive pair of instantaneous velocities computed in the previous step, compute the instantaneous acceleration (acceleration is change in velocity divided by time).
513	For each instantaneous measurement of velocity and acceleration, plug in the following variables.
514	The instantaneous acceleration (a)
515	The instantaneous velocity (v)
516	The weight in kilograms of the barbell (m)
517	Peak Power = m x a x V
518	Select the largest value; this is your peak power.
519	Work
520	As we referenced in the sections discussing Power, Work can be calculated as W = Fd, where F is the average force applied by the athlete to the barbell and d is the displacement of the movement. Work is presented in units of Kilojoules (kJ), which is a measure of Energy. Work can be thought of as the amount of energy the athlete put into the barbell by lifting it against gravity.
521	Time to Peak Power (T2PP)
522	Based on the calculation for Peak Power above (Peak Power = m x a x V), the time to peak power is the duration in seconds it takes to achieve that peak power, based on the start of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as T2PP as an abbreviation in the app.
523	Time to Peak Velocity (T2PV)
524	Based on the calculation for Peak Velocity above, the time to peak velocity is the duration in seconds it takes to achieve that peak velocity, based on the start of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as T2PV as an abbreviation in the app.
525	Velocity at 100ms (V100)
526	The v100 is a new metric that will help to track explosiveness of athletes, among other things.  This is based similarly to calculations above of time to peak velocity and power, but instead measures the velocity at which the bar is moving within the first 100 milliseconds of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as V100 as an abbreviation in the app.
527	Jump Assessment Concepts
528	Jump assessments have special metrics calculated specifically for them. These metrics are built  off of the same tracking technology used for other exercises. Here's what you need to know.
529	Types of Jumping
530	Counter Movement Jump (CMJ)
531	A counter movement jump is defined in Perch as a jump where the athlete begins by standing up straight, dips into a preload by bending knees and hips to a self-selected depth, and then rapidly explodes out of their preload into a vertical jump as high as possible.
532	When performing multiple repetitions, the athlete should land from their previous jump, reset, and return to their original standing position before beginning their next jump.
533	Continuous Jumps
534	A continuous jumping exercise starts similarly to a counter movement jump. The athlete will stand up straight before preloading to a self-selected depth, and then explode into their first repetition of a vertical jump.
535	However, instead of landing and pausing to return to a standing position, the athlete’s landing from the previous jump flows smoothly into the preload of their next jump. Thus, the athlete performs multiple jumps without rest in between. A priority should be minimizing ground contact time while maximizing jump height.
536	Tracking a Jump
537	Because Perch measures 3D position of objects, we track the position of parts of the athlete’s body to track jumps and other non-barbell exercises. The primary object used for tracking jumps is the athlete’s head.
538	To track a jump, Perch uses the position of the athlete's head right before beginning their jump to measure their standing height. When the athlete begins unweighting, for either a CMJ or Continuous Jumps, that marks the beginning of the jump.
539	For continuous jumps, the beginning of each repetition after the athlete’s first is the same as the moment the athlete lands from the previous repetition.
540	After preloading, the athlete explodes upwards into their jump (the propulsive phase). The moment the athlete returns to their original starting height (the end of the propulsive phase) is defined as the moment of takeoff. The athlete’s feet will leave the ground at this moment in time.
541	During the jump, the athlete rises and falls in the air (the flight phase). The apex of the jump can be measured as the highest point the athlete reaches after takeoff. The moment the athlete lands is the moment when the athlete falls back to their original standing height, before decelerating and absorbing the landing.
542	Jump Height
543	Jump height is a measure of displacement. Given the above definitions, Perch measures jump height simply by subtracting the height of the apex of the jump from the athlete’s standing height before the beginning of the jump.
544	Time to Takeoff
545	Time to takeoff is measured as the amount of time elapsed between the beginning of the jump (the start of the unweighting phase) until the moment of takeoff (the end of the propulsive phase).
546	This time includes the full duration of the following jump phases:
547	Unweighting
548	Braking
549	Propulsive
550	Takeoff Velocity
551	Takeoff velocity is a measure of instantaneous velocity at the moment of takeoff (the end of the propulsive phase). This is the speed at which the athlete is moving just before their feet leave the ground after the propulsive phase.
552	RSIMod
553	RSIMod is Jump Height divided by Time to Takeoff. It is reported as a unitless quantity, rather than its true unit of m/s, since it should not be interpreted as a velocity.

564	Displacement/Height – change in the vertical position of the Centre of Mass

596	Concentric Mean Force – average Vertical Force during the Concentric Phase; in Newtons (N)

598	Concentric Mean Power – Average Power during the Concentric Phase; in Watts (W)

601	Concentric Peak Force / BM – Concentric Peak Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)

608	Concentric RPD – RPD from the start of the Concentric Phase to the point when Peak Power occurs; in Watts per second (W/s)
609	Concentric RPD – 100ms – RPD during the first 100ms of the Concentric Phase; in Watts per second (W/s)
610	Concentric RPD – 50ms – RPD during the first 50ms of the Concentric Phase; in Watts per second (W/s)
611	Concentric RPD / BM – Concentric RPD divided by Body Mass; in Watts per second per kilogram (W/s/kg)
612	Concentric RPD-100ms / BM – Concentric RPD 100ms divided by Body Mass; in Watts per second per kilogram (W/s/kg)
613	Concentric RPD-50ms / BM – Concentric RPD 50ms divided by Body Mass; in Watts per second per kilogram (W/s/kg)
614	Concentric Time to Peak Force – time period for the start of the Concentric Phase to the point when Peak Force occurs; in milliseconds (ms)
615	Contraction Time – time period from Start of Movement to Take-off; in milliseconds (ms)
616	Contraction Time:Eccentric Duration – ratio of Contraction Time to Eccentric Duration; as a percentage (%)
617	Countermovement Depth – Maximum Displacement between Start of Movement to Take-off; in centimeters (cm)
618	Displacement at Take-off – Displacement from initial starting position to take-off (i.e., standing upright to leaving the force plates); in centimeters (cm)
619	Eccentric Acceleration Phase Duration – time period of the Eccentric Acceleration Phase (i.e., from Start of Movement to the point when maximum negative Velocity occurs); in seconds (s)
620	Eccentric Braking Impulse – Net Impulse during the Eccentric Braking Phase; in Newton seconds (N s)
621	Eccentric Braking RFD / BM – Eccentric Braking RFD divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per second per kilogram (N/s/kg)
622	Eccentric Braking RFD – RFD over the full Eccentric Braking Phase; in Newtons per second (N/s)
623	Eccentric Braking RFD-100ms – RFD during the first 100ms of the Eccentric Braking Phase; in Newtons per second (N/s)
624	Eccentric Deceleration – Net Impulse during the Eccentric Deceleration Phase; in Newton seconds (N s)
625	Eccentric Deceleration Impulse / BM – Eccentric Deceleration Impulse divided by Body Mass; in Newton seconds per kilogram (N s/kg)
626	Eccentric Deceleration Phase Duration – time period of the Eccentric Deceleration Phase; in seconds (s)
627	Eccentric Deceleration RFD – RFD over the full Eccentric Deceleration Phase; in Newtons per second (N/s)
628	Eccentric Deceleration RFD / BM – Eccentric Deceleration RFD divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per second per kilogram (N/s/kg)
629	Eccentric Duration – time period of the Eccentric Phase; in milliseconds (ms)
630	Eccentric Mean Braking Force – Average Vertical Force during the Eccentric Braking Phase; in Newtons (N)
631	Eccentric Mean Deceleration Force – Average Vertical Force during the Eccentric Deceleration Phase; in Newtons (N)
632	Eccentric Mean Force – Average Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase, equivalent to Body Weight (N); in Newtons (N)
633	Eccentric Mean Power – Average Power during the Eccentric Phase; in Watts (W)
634	Eccentric Mean Power / BM – Eccentric Mean Power divided by Body Mass; in Watts per kilogram (W/kg)
635	Eccentric Peak Force – Maximum Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase; in Newtons (N)
636	Eccentric Peak Force / BM – Eccentric Peak Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
637	Eccentric Peak Power – Maximum Power during the Eccentric Phase; in Watts (W)
638	Eccentric Peak Power:Concentric Peak Power – ratio of Eccentric Peak Power to Concentric Peak Power; unitless
639	Eccentric Peak Velocity – Macimum Velocity during the Eccentric Phase; in milliseconds (ms)
640	Eccentric Unloading Impulse – Net Impulse during the Eccentric Unloading Phase (i.e., from Start of Movement to the start of the Eccentric Deceleration Phase); in Newton seconds (N s)
641	Eccentric Concentric Duration – ratio of Eccentric Duration to Concentric Duration; as a percentage (%)
642	Eccentric Concentric Mean Force Ratio – ratio of Eccentric Mean Force to Concentric Mean Force; as a percentage (%)
643	Flight Time – time period between Take-off and Landing; in milliseconds (ms)
644	Flight Time:Contraction Time – ratio of Flight Time to Contraction Time; unitless
645	Flight Time:Eccentric Duration – ratio of Flight Time to Eccentric Duration; unitless
646	Force at Peak Power – Vertical Force at the point when Peak Power occurs; in Newtons (N)
647	Force at Zero Velocity – Vertical Force at the point when zero Velocity occurs prior to Take-off; in Newtons (N)
648	Force at Zero Velocity / BM – Force at Zero Velocity divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
649	Jump Height (Flight Time) – Jump Height calculated from Flight Time; in centimeters (cm)
650	Jump Height (Flight Time) in Inches – Jump Height (Flight Time) converted to inches; in inches (in)
651	Jump Height (FT) Relative Landing RFD – Landing RFD divided by Jump Height (Flight Time); in Newtons per second per centimeter (N/s/cm)
652	Jump Height (FT) Relative Peak Landing Force – Peak Landing Force divided by Jump Height (Flight Time); in Newtons per centimeter (N/cm)
653	Lower-Limb Stiffness – Change in Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase divided by Countermovement Depth; in Newtons per meter (N/m)
654	Mean Eccentric+Concentric Power:Time – Mean Power between Start of Movement and Take-off, divided by Contraction Time; in Watts per second (W/s)
655	Minimum Eccentric Force – Minimum Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase; in Newtons (N)
656	Movement Start to Peak Force – Time Period between Start of Movement and the point when Peak Vertical Force occurs prior to Take-off; in seconds (s)
657	Movement Start to Peak Power – Time Period between Start of Movement and the point when Peak Power occurs prior to Take-off; in seconds (s)
658	P1 Concentric Impulse – Net Impulse during the first 50% of the Concentric Phase (time-wise); in Newton seconds (N s)
659	P2 Concentric Impulse – Net Impulse during the second 50% of the Concentric Phase (time-wise); in Newton seconds (N s)
660	P2 Concentric Impulse:P1 Concentric Impulse – Ratio of P2 Concentric Impulse to P1 Concentric Impulse; unitless
661	Peak Net Take-off Force / BM – Maximum Vertical Force between Start of Movement and Take-off, - Body Weight, and divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
662	Peak Power – Maximum Power during the Concentric Phase; in Watts (W)
663	Peak Power / BM – Peak Power divided by Body Mass; in Watts per kilogram (W/kg)
664	Peak Take-off Acceleration – Maximum Acceleration of the Center of Mass between Start of Movement and Take-off; in Meters per second squared (m/s2)
665	Positive Impulse – Net Impulse during the entire repetition (eccentric, concentric, and landing combined); in Newton seconds (N s)
666	Positive Take-off Impulse – Net Impulse during Take-off (eccentric and concentric phases combined); in Newton seconds (N s)
667	RSI-modified – Jump Height (Flight Time) divided by Contraction Time; in meters per second (m/s)
668	RSI-modified (Imp-Mom) – Jump Height (Imp-Mom) divided by Contraction Time; in meters per second (m/s)
669	Landing Phase Metrics
670	Jump Height (Imp-Dis) – Maximum Displacement of the Center of Mass between Take-off and Landing; in centimeters (cm)
671	Jump Height (Imp-Mom) – Jump Height calculated from the Velocity of the Center of Mass at the instant of Take-off and Body Mass; in centimeters (cm)
672	Jump Height (Imp-Mom) in Inches – Jump Height (Imp-Mom) converted to inches; in inches (in)
673	Landing Impulse – Absolute Impulse from Landing to the point when Peak Landing Force occur; in Newton seconds (N s)
674	Landing Net Peak Force / BM – Maximum Vertical Force after Landing, - Body Weight, and divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
675	Landing RFD – RFD between Landing and the point when Peak Landing Force occurs; in Newtons per second (N/s)
676	Landing RFD 50ms – RFD of the first 50ms following Landing; in Newtons per second (N/s)
677	Mean Landing Power – Average Power between Landing and the end of the rep; in Watts (W)
678	Peak Landing Acceleration – Maximum Acceleration of the Center of Mass between Landing and the end of the rep; in meters per second squared (m/s2)
679	Peak Landing Force – Maximum Vertical Force after Landing; in Newtons (N)
680	Peak Landing Force / BM – Peak Landing Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
681	Peak Landing Power – Maximum Power between Landing and the end of the rep; in Watts (W)
682	Peak Landing Velocity – Maximum Velocity of the Center of Mass between Landing and the end of the rep; in meters per second (m/s)
683	Take-off Peak Force – Maximum Vertical Force between Start of Movement and Take-off; in Newtons (N)
684	Take-off Peak Force / BM – Take-off Peak Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
685	Time to Braking Phase – time period between Start of Movement and the beginning of the Eccentric Braking Phase;  in seconds (s)
686	Total Work – Integration of Power (i.e., area under the Power-Time curve) between Start of Movement and Take-off; in Joules (J)
687	Velocity at Peak Power – Velocity of the Center of Mass at the point when Peak Power between Start of Movement and Take-off occurs; in meters per second (m/s)
688	Vertical Velocity at Take-off – Velocity of the Center of Mass at the point when Take-off occurs; in meters per second (m/s)
689	For more information on jump metrics, visit the VALD ForceDecks Technical Glossary.
690	To access the ForceDecks user guide, click HERE.

692	To access the NordBord user guide, click HERE.

695	Catapult | GPS tracking devices measure various forms of athletic workload in field-based sports (e.g., high-velocity sprint exposures, heart rate, distance covered, and total number of accelerations and decelerations).
696	Catapult OpenField | Online platform used to access GPS performance analytics and create data visualizations.
697	Kitman Labs | Athlete management system (AMS) that acts as a central data storage site for multiple technologies. Allows for scalable data analysis and visualization across Baylor sport teams.
698	Perch | Camera-based system that utilizes both hardware and software for Velocity Based Training (VBT) and weight room performance monitoring.

BAYLOR ATHLETICS
APPLIED PERFORMANCE OPERATIONS GUIDE
## [Heading 1] PREPARING CHAMPIONS FOR LIFE
INTRODUCTION
Participating in 19 varsity sports, Baylor student-athletes compete at the highest level on the field, on the court, and in the classroom, consistently ranking among the Big 12’s and nation’s best. Baylor Athletics stands in support of the university’s important mission to educate men and women for worldwide leadership and service by integrating academic excellence and Christian commitment within a caring community. This mission informs our day-to-day efforts through one simple purpose: PREPARE CHAMPIONS FOR LIFE.
DEFINING CHAMPIONS
In the context of athletics, the word “champion” evokes images of a game-winning shot, a feat of physical strength, or a trophy hoisted high by a victorious team; but it has much deeper roots. One of the earliest definitions is as “one who fights on behalf of others” (circa 1300), and later “to fight for, defend, or protect” (circa 1820).
When we say we will “Prepare Champions for Life,” we are calling to that deeper sense of the word. Each year, more than 500 student-athletes are on campus representing the GREEN and GOLD. Our job is to educate and prepare these individuals in all aspects of their life, so they leave Waco with a depth of understanding of what transforms an individual into a champion.
No team or individual is successful without a successful process – a championship process. Baylor Athletics focuses on four key areas of development to ensure our student-athletes receive the training and support we are uniquely equipped to provide.
Our championship process rests on these four pillars:
ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT
ATHLETIC SUCCESS
SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
SPIRITUAL GROWTH
## [Heading 1] ONE STANDARD. ONE ACCORD.
Baylor Athletics’ ability to carry out the vision of Preparing Champions for Life hinges on a collective commitment to live by ONE STANDARD – to faithfully steward the authentic pursuit of competitive excellence through Christ. In upholding this standard, the department has committed to be in ONE ACCORD on six scripturally based operating principles and 18 associated core values.
We will do our serviceable and personal best. – Ecclesiastes 9:10
Purpose | Perseverance | Preeminence
We will commit to principled innovation. – Romans 12:2
Reflection | Aspiration | Advancement
We will master fundamentals and pursue excellence. – Ephesians 2:10
Intent | Equip | Championships
We will treat one another with dignity and respect. – Colossians 3:12-14
Service | Love | Truth
We will welcome vulnerability and accountability. – Psalm 139:23-24
Inclusivity | Humility | Trust
We will make all decisions in accordance with governing regulations. – Galatians 6:9
Virtue | Transparent | Vigilance
## [Heading 1] HEALTH & WELLNESS
ATHLETICS PERFORMANCE
The mission of Baylor University Athletics Performance is to set the standard for elite preparation, which will serve as a bridge to life-long student-athlete success while achieving competitive excellence.
ATHLETIC MEDICINE
Baylor University Athletic Medicine (BUAM) promotes health and safety in sport while maintaining an environment focusing on the Christian mission of Baylor University. BUAM’s objective is to serve the healthcare needs of Baylor student-athletes promptly and precisely to allow them the opportunity to achieve success in athletics and life.
PERFORMANCE NUTRITION
Baylor Performance Nutrition guides the practical execution of evidence-based nutrition strategies to optimize athletic performance and foster lifelong healthy behaviors. The department provides individual consultations, hosts team education sessions, evaluates and informs student-athletes about supplements, performs body composition and bone density assessments, and oversees the student-athlete training table (Beauchamp Athletics Nutrition Center) and fueling stations.
MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES
Baylor Athletics Mental Health Services (AMHS) is dedicated to the growth and development of student-athletes through providing the highest quality mental health care. Mental health professionals are available to meet with student-athletes to help them deal with a wide variety of issues that may arise during their collegiate experience. Professional counselors are trained to help student-athletes identify and change ways of thinking or behaving that are potentially contributing to their distress or impairing their functioning. AMHS empowers Baylor student-athletes to discuss their personal concerns in a confidential and nonjudgmental setting.
## [Heading 1] APPLIED PERFORMANCE
MISSION
Operating within the Baylor Athletics Health and Wellness Department, BAYLOR APPLIED PERFORMANCE drives the elite performance of championship-level athletic programs by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships. In fulfilling this mission, Applied Performance aims to enable the high-performance team (Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, Mental Health Services, and sport coaching staffs) to answer team- and/or technology-specific questions, ask better questions based on presented evidence; and discover new questions.
OPERATING PRINCIPLES
Athlete Monitoring and analysis
Use various objective and subjective measures related to health and performance across each season phase (pre-season, in-season, post-season, and off-season).
Provide information that supports the Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine staff to determine appropriate training and return-to-performance (RTP) periodization with reference to typical training and competition demands.
Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance
Identify sport- and position-specific key performance indicators (KPIs).
Conduct athlete evaluations for diagnostic screening, performance testing, and KPI threshold identification.
Performance Team Collaboration
Bring together all members of the high-performance team through effective knowledge dissemination.
Provide data to inform the decision-making process throughout Health and Wellness.
Research and Development
In collaboration with on-campus faculty, conduct internal and external research on the latest performance technologies and trends within intercollegiate athletics.
Provide the high-performance team with knowledge to implement best practices for improving student-athlete performance and minimizing injury risk.

TECHNOLOGY WORKFLOWS
Step 1: Pre-Activity
Charging Equipment
Units and Dock(s)
Connect devices into dock ports
Connect dock to power supply
Once charging, devices should display a red light on top
Devices are fully charged once red light turns green
Receiver(s)
C-Type cable inserts at bottom of receiver
USB end can be attached into wall attachment
Light on side of receiver will turn red indicating it is charging
Light will turn green once receiver is fully charged
Setting Device Alarm(s)
Connect devices into dock(s)
Connect dock to computer
Open the OpenField console
Press ignition (silver button) on dock(s)
Select “Device Manager” from tile/home page
Confirm that number of connected units matches the number of units that are in the dock(s)
Click “Select All” at the bottom
Select “Execute” next to “Set Alarm Time” command
Enter desired alarm time (in military time)
Confirm that all devices received the command; check right window
Press ignition (silver button) to turn off dock(s)
DO NOT REMOVE UNITS WHILE DOCKS ARE ON. This will automatically turn the units on.
Step 2: Create Activity
Creating a Session
Launch OpenField console and click “Start” on the tile/home page
Right click in the timeline and select “New Activity”
Enter activity name
For “Device Type,” select “GPS”
Assign appropriate “Day Code” and tags
Click “Create Activity”
Step 3: Equipment Set-up
Running a Live Session
Power on Vector Master Receiver (press and hold until green light appears)
To power off, press and hold
When turquoise light is solid, the receiver’s Wi-Fi will broadcast
If using secondary receiver(s), verify that each has a turquoise light
Blinking turquoise means that the receiver is communicating with and sending data to the Vector Master Receiver
Solid turquoise means that the Vector Secondary Receiver has found and connected to Master but is NOT transferring data
Red means Secondary Receiver has NOT found and connected to Master
Connect laptop or iPad to receiver’s Wi-Fi
Hit play button at top right of screen
Confirm that athlete names are populating under “Active Players” window on right
Step 4: Period Management
Adding Periods
Option 1
Select “+” to add a period
Click on period in timeline
Click “All” in Active Players window or select specific athletes
Click “+PIP”
“PIP” window at top right of window should show athletes were placed in period
To stop all live periods, select the slashed circle icon
Option 2 (RECOMMENDED)
Select “All” in Active Players window
Select “+Period”
“PIP” window at top right of window should show athletes were placed in period
To stop all live periods, select the slashed circle icon
Step 5: Post-Session Import
Downloading and Synchronization
Connect units into dock(s)
Connect dock(s) to computer
Launch OpenField console
Press ignition (silver button) on dock(s); white light should appear on front of devices
Select “Data Transfer” from tile/home page
Devices should begin transferring session data; if not, select “Begin Transfer” at top of window
Once all entries display “Finished” under the status column, select “Full Sync”
When full sync is completed, refresh OpenField Cloud (website) to access session data
Step 6: Post-Import
Editing an Activity (Console)
Launch OpenField console
Select “Last Activity” from tile/home page
Cleaning Data (Console)
Right click on athlete in “PIP” window in top right
Select “Graph” from drop down list
Right click on athlete’s name at bottom right of timeline window to ensure metric to be flagged is displayed (e.g., “Live Parameter” -> “Velocity”)
Locate start and end of data spike on graph
Utilize proper shortcut by hovering over information/help icon
Tagging Activity (Cloud)
Locate “Settings” at top left of Cloud window
Select “Tags” tab from left of window
Select appropriate tag group from left column and tag category from right column
Click on selection to tag
Click, drag, and drop tag from left column to selection in right column
Download/Email PDF Report (Cloud)
Choose dashboard to download
Right click on dashboard tab
Select “Export PDF”
Adjust formatting
Select either “Download” or “Send Email”
Enter email if you select “Send Email”
Click “Save and Export”

Preparation and Set-Up
Ensure the DynaMo device is charged and ready for use.
Connect the DynaMo device to the tablet or computer via Bluetooth. Make sure the VALD Performance app is installed and updated on the device.
Gather any necessary attachments or accessories required for the specific test you plan to conduct.
Participant Registration
Open the VALD Performance app on the tablet or computer.
Create a new participant profile if it's the first time the athlete is being tested. Input all necessary details, such as name, date of birth, sport, and position.
If the participant is already registered, select their profile from the database.
Device Calibration
Follow the on-screen instructions to calibrate the DynaMo device. This usually involves zeroing the sensors to ensure accurate force readings.
Confirm that the calibration process is complete before proceeding to the testing phase.
Testing Protocol Set-Up
Select the appropriate testing protocol from the app, such as grip strength, push-pull strength, or other functional assessments.
Adjust the device settings to match the specific requirements of the selected protocol (e.g., duration of the test, number of repetitions).
Participant Positioning
Instruct the participant on the correct positioning and technique for the test. Ensure they understand the procedure and expected effort level.
Position the participant correctly according to the test protocol. This may involve specific body postures or the use of attachments to the DynaMo device.
Conducting the Test
Explain the test procedure to the participant, including how to perform the actions and the importance of maximal effort.
Start the test using the app interface. The participant will then perform the required actions (e.g., maximal grip contraction).
Monitor the participant’s form and provide encouragement and instructions as needed throughout the test.
Data Collection and Analysis
Once the test is completed, review the collected data on the app. Key metrics typically include peak force, average force, and rate of force development.
Ensure the data is saved to the participant’s profile for future reference and longitudinal tracking.
Feedback and Recommendations
Provide immediate feedback to the participant regarding their performance. Highlight areas of strength and opportunities for improvement.
Discuss any recommendations for training or rehabilitation based on the test results.
Post-Test Procedures
Safely remove any attachments and assist the participant in getting off the device if necessary.
Sanitize the device and any used accessories according to hygiene protocols.
Data Export and Reporting
Export the test results from the VALD Performance app if required. The data can typically be exported in various formats (e.g., CSV, PDF).
Generate and distribute reports to relevant stakeholders.
Prior to Testing
Log in – Log in to ForceDecks Jump
Confirm settings – Confirm the following settings:
Layout > Operational Mode is set to “Shared”
Layout > Show Profile Selection Pane is set to “Always”
Platforms > Sequenced Platform Count is set to “1”
Platforms > Platform Assignment is correct for your plate setup
Platforms > Auto Test Export Folder is the same folder as ForceDecks
Starting a Test
Confirm test queue – Double click profile names to add them to the testing queue.
Start testing – Click “Play” button.
Confirm weighing – Click “Weigh Start” or “Start” to confirm your weighing option.
Zero sensors – Ensure nothing is touching the plates before allowing the plates to zero.
Recording a Test
Assume starting position – Ask the first individual (profile) in the testing queue to assume the starting position on the plates.
Perform rep – Instruct the individual to perform the required movement/jump.
Repeat rep – Have the individual pause for 2-3 seconds, then repeat the movement/jump for the required number of reps.
Select next individual (profile) – Select the next individual in the testing queue and repeat steps 1-4. Up to 16 profiles may be tested before stopping the recording.
Stop recording – Click “Stop” button to examine all results.
Review – Review and edit results as required.
Save – Click “Save” to select reps, apply tags and notes; or click “Save All” to save.
