Other
IMA
Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) is a set of metrics that measures athlete micro movements and direction regardless of unit orientation. Athlete movements can be quantified into low, medium and high intensity athlete movements zones that are used to construct profiles of athletes’ movements and to recognize biomechanical red flags.
IMA gives indoor and outdoor sports the ability to track acceleration count, deceleration count, asymmetrical loading, change of direction (COD) count – left and right, free running event count, free running total time, average stride rate, impacts, and jump count.
IMA allows the end user to collect and analyze acceleration- and deceleration-based data without the use of a GPS system. It is beneficial for indoor sessions in which a user cannot collect GPS data. It is also beneficial for breaking down movements into micro movements which can further be analyzed for performance insights.
3D Position
Perch uses a 3D camera to directly measure the position of objects in the field of view of the camera. Every image that the Perch camera captures contains information about how far away objects are from the camera itself.
Using a complex tracking pipeline developed by engineers at Perch, the camera processes the image to find the objects we’re interested in (namely, a barbell, parts of the body, etc.). Once the object is located in the image, the device will use the distance data from the 3D camera and some geometry to triangulate where the object is in 3D space. Otherwise known as determining the 3D coordinate of the object for this particular point in time.
3D position, as its name suggests, consists of three spatial dimensions. The names we use for these dimensions are X, Y, and Z. We define Z as up and down (parallel to gravity), X as forwards and backwards (in the perspective of the athlete), and Y as side to side (in the perspective of the athlete).
3D Path
The 3D path of an object – in our case, usually a barbell – is nothing more than a sequence of 3D coordinates with time stamps. By processing images rapidly as the 3D camera captures them, we collect many 3D coordinates and collect them together to form a 3D path.
The 3D path represents precisely where in 3D space an object moved over time. This is the core data that Perch captures, and every other metric is calculated using this 3D path.
Displacement
Displacement is simply calculated by subtracting a starting 3D position and from an ending position. If you isolate only one of the axes, for example the Z axis, you then have the vertical displacement between those positions. For example, in the case of a back squat, the displacement on the Z axis can be interpreted as the squat depth.
Velocity
The equation for velocity is always the same: displacement (aka. distance) divided by time. Since we are able to go from 3D position to 3D Path and finally calculate displacement, we’re halfway there. Every 3D coordinate also has a corresponding time associated with it, and we can subtract the times starting and ending 3D coordinates to calculate the amount of time elapsed between those two positions.
By dividing the displacement by the time that elapsed between them, you are calculating velocity.
Mean Velocity
Mean velocity (or average velocity) as used in VBT is defined as the average velocity of a complete movement (e.g. the concentric portion of a rep).
Calculating mean velocity is exactly the same as calculating any other velocity, except the start and end 3D positions you choose are the beginning and end of the movement respectively.
For example, to calculate the concentric mean velocity (on the Z axis) of a rep, we perform three calculations:
We subtract the Z value of the coordinate of the bottom of the rep (the beginning of the concentric movement) from the highest point at the end of the rep (the final coordinate of the concentric movement) to calculate the displacement.
We subtract the times of the same two coordinates chosen above to calculate the duration of the concentric movement.
Finally, we divide the displacement by the duration to get the velocity.
Concentric and Eccentric Mean Velocity are both captured in the system and are registered separately – one will not impact the other.
Peak Velocity
Calculating peak velocity is once again very similar to other velocity calculations, however it differs in selection of the coordinates.
Peak velocity is defined as the greatest instantaneous velocity during a movement. Here, “instantaneous” means between two consecutive coordinates. Naturally, there is some amount of time between each coordinate we measure, so using two adjacent coordinates is not truly instantaneous, but is sufficiently close.
As an example, to find the peak concentric velocity (on the Z axis), we do the following:
Compute the instantaneous velocity using every pair of consecutive coordinates from the lowest to the highest point of the movement (following the same procedure as defined above)
The largest of these instantaneous velocities is your peak concentric velocity
Eccentric Time
Eccentric time is tracking the amount of time, in seconds, it takes to complete the eccentric portion of the movement. This is not displayed on the tablet for Olympic lifts or for jumps.
We subtract the Z value of the coordinate of the top of the rep (the beginning of the eccentric movement) from the lowest point at the end of the rep (the final coordinate of the eccentric movement). We subtract the times of the same two coordinates to calculate the duration of the eccentric movement.
Power
The equation for power is defined as Work divided by time: P = W / t
In our case, the force is how much force the athlete is applying to the barbell. While we’ve already covered how we can calculate velocity (the Vterm), we can’t directly measure the force. However, we can calculate it in a couple different ways depending on the context.
Mean Power
Mean power can be described as the average amount of power over the duration of the movement. To calculate, we can reuse the mean velocity we’ve already calculated above for the V term in our power equations.
The force (F) in our equation is similarly the average force applied by the athlete during the movement. Because the bar is at rest before and after the movement, the average force is equal to the force required to oppose gravity (aka, the force of gravity) on the barbell. As such, the force is the mass of the barbell (in kilograms) multiplied by the acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/s).
With the math established, calculating mean power is as simple as substituting the mass of the barbell (converted to kilograms, m) and the mean velocity (in meters per second, V) into the following equation: Mean Power = m x 9.8 x V
Peak Power
Calculating peak power requires a bit more complexity, as was the case with peak velocity.
In order to calculate the peak power output for a movement, we calculate the instantaneous power at every point during the movement and select the largest.
Here is the general procedure for how we calculate peak power for a concentric movement:
Using the same procedure as in peak velocity, calculate the instantaneous velocity for every pair of points in the movement.
Using every consecutive pair of instantaneous velocities computed in the previous step, compute the instantaneous acceleration (acceleration is change in velocity divided by time).
For each instantaneous measurement of velocity and acceleration, plug in the following variables.
The instantaneous acceleration (a)
The instantaneous velocity (v)
The weight in kilograms of the barbell (m)
Peak Power = m x a x V
Select the largest value; this is your peak power.
Work
As we referenced in the sections discussing Power, Work can be calculated as W = Fd, where F is the average force applied by the athlete to the barbell and d is the displacement of the movement. Work is presented in units of Kilojoules (kJ), which is a measure of Energy. Work can be thought of as the amount of energy the athlete put into the barbell by lifting it against gravity.
Time to Peak Power (T2PP)
Based on the calculation for Peak Power above (Peak Power = m x a x V), the time to peak power is the duration in seconds it takes to achieve that peak power, based on the start of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as T2PP as an abbreviation in the app.
Time to Peak Velocity (T2PV)
Based on the calculation for Peak Velocity above, the time to peak velocity is the duration in seconds it takes to achieve that peak velocity, based on the start of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as T2PV as an abbreviation in the app.
Velocity at 100ms (V100)
The v100 is a new metric that will help to track explosiveness of athletes, among other things.  This is based similarly to calculations above of time to peak velocity and power, but instead measures the velocity at which the bar is moving within the first 100 milliseconds of the concentric portion of the rep.  This is displayed as V100 as an abbreviation in the app.
Jump Assessment Concepts
Jump assessments have special metrics calculated specifically for them. These metrics are built  off of the same tracking technology used for other exercises. Here's what you need to know.
Types of Jumping
Counter Movement Jump (CMJ)
A counter movement jump is defined in Perch as a jump where the athlete begins by standing up straight, dips into a preload by bending knees and hips to a self-selected depth, and then rapidly explodes out of their preload into a vertical jump as high as possible.
When performing multiple repetitions, the athlete should land from their previous jump, reset, and return to their original standing position before beginning their next jump.
Continuous Jumps
A continuous jumping exercise starts similarly to a counter movement jump. The athlete will stand up straight before preloading to a self-selected depth, and then explode into their first repetition of a vertical jump.
However, instead of landing and pausing to return to a standing position, the athlete’s landing from the previous jump flows smoothly into the preload of their next jump. Thus, the athlete performs multiple jumps without rest in between. A priority should be minimizing ground contact time while maximizing jump height.
Tracking a Jump
Because Perch measures 3D position of objects, we track the position of parts of the athlete’s body to track jumps and other non-barbell exercises. The primary object used for tracking jumps is the athlete’s head.
To track a jump, Perch uses the position of the athlete's head right before beginning their jump to measure their standing height. When the athlete begins unweighting, for either a CMJ or Continuous Jumps, that marks the beginning of the jump.
For continuous jumps, the beginning of each repetition after the athlete’s first is the same as the moment the athlete lands from the previous repetition.
After preloading, the athlete explodes upwards into their jump (the propulsive phase). The moment the athlete returns to their original starting height (the end of the propulsive phase) is defined as the moment of takeoff. The athlete’s feet will leave the ground at this moment in time.
During the jump, the athlete rises and falls in the air (the flight phase). The apex of the jump can be measured as the highest point the athlete reaches after takeoff. The moment the athlete lands is the moment when the athlete falls back to their original standing height, before decelerating and absorbing the landing.
Jump Height
Jump height is a measure of displacement. Given the above definitions, Perch measures jump height simply by subtracting the height of the apex of the jump from the athlete’s standing height before the beginning of the jump.
Time to Takeoff
Time to takeoff is measured as the amount of time elapsed between the beginning of the jump (the start of the unweighting phase) until the moment of takeoff (the end of the propulsive phase).
This time includes the full duration of the following jump phases:
Unweighting
Braking
Propulsive
Takeoff Velocity
Takeoff velocity is a measure of instantaneous velocity at the moment of takeoff (the end of the propulsive phase). This is the speed at which the athlete is moving just before their feet leave the ground after the propulsive phase.
RSIMod
RSIMod is Jump Height divided by Time to Takeoff. It is reported as a unitless quantity, rather than its true unit of m/s, since it should not be interpreted as a velocity.

Technical Definitions
Absolute – the magnitude of a given value (irrespective of being positive or negative)
Acceleration – rate of change in velocity over time of the centre of mass (m/s2)
Asymmetry – a relative measurement of difference between two sided values expressed as a percentage. Calculated as (Left Metric value – Right Metric value) / maximum of (Left Metric value or Right Metric value) x 100
Body Mass (BM) – measure of mass collected during weighing (kg)
Body Weight (BW) – mass captured during the ‘Weigh Profile’ stage (N)
Center of Mass (CoM) – the balance point of the body that mass is distributed about
Displacement/Height – change in the vertical position of the Centre of Mass
Force – strength as an attribute of physical action or movement
Impulse (Absolute Impulse) – integration (area under the curve) of Force over a given period time period (Ns)
Impulse (Net Impulse) – area under the force curve over a given time period but only above body weight (Ns)
Impulse (Positive Impulse) – area under the curve from the start of movement to take off (i.e.: eccentric and concentric phases combined) but only above body weight (Ns)
Left Force – the vertical Force component measured from the left force plate (N)
Left Metric – metric calculated using only the Left Force
Maximum/Peak – the highest or largest value within a dataset or phase
Mean – average of all data points within a dataset or phase, including the start and end of the phase
Minimum – the single lowest value within a dataset or phase
Power – the work rate a force exerts on an object, calculated as force x velocity (W)
Recording – an entire force-time dataset from the time Start Recording is clicked until Stop Recording is clicked
Rep – short for repetition, a period of time in a recording during which a single instance of a test is performed
Rate of Force Development (RFD) - change in force over a given time period or phase (N/s)
Right Force – the vertical Force component measured from the right force plate (N)
Right Metric – metric calculated using only the Right Force
Rate of Power Development (RPD) – change in power over a given time period or phase (W/s)
Velocity – change in center of mass position over time (m/s)
Vertical Force – the vertical force component measured from a single force plate or combined from both (N)

Braking Phase Duration:Concentric Duration – ratio of Braking Phase Duration to Concentric Phase Duration; unitless
Braking Phase Duration:Contraction Time – ratio of Braking Phase Duration to Contraction Time; unitless

Eccentric Mean Power – Average Power during the Eccentric Phase; in Watts (W)

Eccentric Peak Force – Maximum Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase; in Newtons (N)
Eccentric Peak Force / BM – Eccentric Peak Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
Eccentric Peak Power – Maximum Power during the Eccentric Phase; in Watts (W)
Eccentric Peak Power:Concentric Peak Power – ratio of Eccentric Peak Power to Concentric Peak Power; unitless
Eccentric Peak Velocity – Macimum Velocity during the Eccentric Phase; in milliseconds (ms)
Eccentric Unloading Impulse – Net Impulse during the Eccentric Unloading Phase (i.e., from Start of Movement to the start of the Eccentric Deceleration Phase); in Newton seconds (N s)
Eccentric Concentric Duration – ratio of Eccentric Duration to Concentric Duration; as a percentage (%)
Eccentric Concentric Mean Force Ratio – ratio of Eccentric Mean Force to Concentric Mean Force; as a percentage (%)
Flight Time – time period between Take-off and Landing; in milliseconds (ms)
Flight Time:Contraction Time – ratio of Flight Time to Contraction Time; unitless
Flight Time:Eccentric Duration – ratio of Flight Time to Eccentric Duration; unitless
Force at Peak Power – Vertical Force at the point when Peak Power occurs; in Newtons (N)
Force at Zero Velocity – Vertical Force at the point when zero Velocity occurs prior to Take-off; in Newtons (N)
Force at Zero Velocity / BM – Force at Zero Velocity divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
Jump Height (Flight Time) – Jump Height calculated from Flight Time; in centimeters (cm)
Jump Height (Flight Time) in Inches – Jump Height (Flight Time) converted to inches; in inches (in)
Jump Height (FT) Relative Landing RFD – Landing RFD divided by Jump Height (Flight Time); in Newtons per second per centimeter (N/s/cm)
Jump Height (FT) Relative Peak Landing Force – Peak Landing Force divided by Jump Height (Flight Time); in Newtons per centimeter (N/cm)
Lower-Limb Stiffness – Change in Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase divided by Countermovement Depth; in Newtons per meter (N/m)
Mean Eccentric+Concentric Power:Time – Mean Power between Start of Movement and Take-off, divided by Contraction Time; in Watts per second (W/s)
Minimum Eccentric Force – Minimum Vertical Force during the Eccentric Phase; in Newtons (N)
Movement Start to Peak Force – Time Period between Start of Movement and the point when Peak Vertical Force occurs prior to Take-off; in seconds (s)
Movement Start to Peak Power – Time Period between Start of Movement and the point when Peak Power occurs prior to Take-off; in seconds (s)
P1 Concentric Impulse – Net Impulse during the first 50% of the Concentric Phase (time-wise); in Newton seconds (N s)
P2 Concentric Impulse – Net Impulse during the second 50% of the Concentric Phase (time-wise); in Newton seconds (N s)
P2 Concentric Impulse:P1 Concentric Impulse – Ratio of P2 Concentric Impulse to P1 Concentric Impulse; unitless
Peak Net Take-off Force / BM – Maximum Vertical Force between Start of Movement and Take-off, - Body Weight, and divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
Peak Power – Maximum Power during the Concentric Phase; in Watts (W)
Peak Power / BM – Peak Power divided by Body Mass; in Watts per kilogram (W/kg)
Peak Take-off Acceleration – Maximum Acceleration of the Center of Mass between Start of Movement and Take-off; in Meters per second squared (m/s2)
Positive Impulse – Net Impulse during the entire repetition (eccentric, concentric, and landing combined); in Newton seconds (N s)
Positive Take-off Impulse – Net Impulse during Take-off (eccentric and concentric phases combined); in Newton seconds (N s)
RSI-modified – Jump Height (Flight Time) divided by Contraction Time; in meters per second (m/s)
RSI-modified (Imp-Mom) – Jump Height (Imp-Mom) divided by Contraction Time; in meters per second (m/s)
Landing Phase Metrics
Jump Height (Imp-Dis) – Maximum Displacement of the Center of Mass between Take-off and Landing; in centimeters (cm)
Jump Height (Imp-Mom) – Jump Height calculated from the Velocity of the Center of Mass at the instant of Take-off and Body Mass; in centimeters (cm)
Jump Height (Imp-Mom) in Inches – Jump Height (Imp-Mom) converted to inches; in inches (in)
Landing Impulse – Absolute Impulse from Landing to the point when Peak Landing Force occur; in Newton seconds (N s)
Landing Net Peak Force / BM – Maximum Vertical Force after Landing, - Body Weight, and divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
Landing RFD – RFD between Landing and the point when Peak Landing Force occurs; in Newtons per second (N/s)
Landing RFD 50ms – RFD of the first 50ms following Landing; in Newtons per second (N/s)
Mean Landing Power – Average Power between Landing and the end of the rep; in Watts (W)
Peak Landing Acceleration – Maximum Acceleration of the Center of Mass between Landing and the end of the rep; in meters per second squared (m/s2)
Peak Landing Force – Maximum Vertical Force after Landing; in Newtons (N)
Peak Landing Force / BM – Peak Landing Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
Peak Landing Power – Maximum Power between Landing and the end of the rep; in Watts (W)
Peak Landing Velocity – Maximum Velocity of the Center of Mass between Landing and the end of the rep; in meters per second (m/s)
Take-off Peak Force – Maximum Vertical Force between Start of Movement and Take-off; in Newtons (N)
Take-off Peak Force / BM – Take-off Peak Force divided by Body Mass; in Newtons per kilogram (N/kg)
Time to Braking Phase – time period between Start of Movement and the beginning of the Eccentric Braking Phase;  in seconds (s)
Total Work – Integration of Power (i.e., area under the Power-Time curve) between Start of Movement and Take-off; in Joules (J)
Velocity at Peak Power – Velocity of the Center of Mass at the point when Peak Power between Start of Movement and Take-off occurs; in meters per second (m/s)

=== NCAA PLAN.md ===
# Plan: Performance Technology Best Practices (NCAA SSI)

Draft 2026-10-04, for agreement with Chris Ruf by **2026-10-14** (charter step 1).
Source material and the full gap analysis: `docs/SOURCES.md`.

## What this document is

A Baylor best-practices document that puts the NCAA SSI *Performance Technologies
Recommendations: Responsible Use in Collegiate Athletics* (CSMAS/SSI, March 2026) into
practice in four areas Chris signs off on:

1. Technology adoption plan
2. Athlete consent
3. Vendor data contracts
4. Staff-transition continuity

**Done means:** Chris signs it off, and it is in use by 2026-12-16.

## Three decisions to get from Chris first

Everything below assumes the recommendation in each. If he picks the other option,
the outline changes, but the schedule doesn't.

| # | Decision | Recommendation | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Best-practice guide or formal department policy? | **Guide plus procedures and forms**, with a one-page policy statement only if Chris wants one | At the 2026-07-30 meeting, leadership preferred "flexible best-practice documents over rigid formal policy". UT chose formal policy (SMED-8055); we can follow its structure without its formality. |
| 2 | How does this relate to the Software & Technology Management Framework (draft, 08-14)? | **This document is the framework's "Version 1" content.** The framework keeps the request and review process (SSI Rec 4). This document supplies what the framework marks "planned for Version 1": the working group, consent, education, the transfer protocol, the feedback loop | Avoids two documents covering the same process. The framework's request process is already built. |
| 3 | Scope: only the four areas, or the four plus education? | **Four areas plus a short education section** | SSI calls education "foundational for informed consent" (Rec 2), so consent can't stand without it. Keep education to who, how often and what topics, not a curriculum. |

## Proposed outline of the document

0. **Purpose and scope.** SSI basis, definitions (SSI's own, as UT does), who it applies to.
1. **Governance.** A standing Performance Technology Working Group: multidisciplinary, with student-athlete members (SSI Rec 1.1). Annual review of this document. Named owner. Medical authority over return-to-play stays with Athletic Medicine (Rec 3.3).
2. **Technology adoption.** Points to the framework's request and review process (Rec 4). Adds only what it lacks: the "start from the question" rule (Iowa State's intake form), and one scoring instrument. Today the March checklist and the framework scorecard compete; reconcile them into one.
3. **Athlete consent and education.**
   - Notice versus consent: which data needs opt-in consent, and which is unavoidable but disclosed. Webinar line: venue tracking is unavoidable, a wearable needs consent.
   - Consent form, built from the March template: voluntary, withdraw without penalty, retention, transfer.
   - Disclosure when de-identified data goes to vendor norm-building.
   - Annual re-consent, and re-consent when a new technology is introduced.
   - Where consent records live.
   - Annual education by group (Rec 2.1–2.3).
4. **Data management.**
   - Ownership, storage, access, and who may interpret and communicate data (Rec 3, 3.1).
   - The physiologic versus performance data classification.
   - Collect only what is used ("if you're not doing anything with it, don't collect it").
   - Transfer-athlete protocol (Rec 3.2).
5. **Vendor data contracts.**
   - A standard data addendum or clause checklist: ownership, permitted use, storage and jurisdiction, AI training, downstream sharing, data-for-discount or norm-pooling terms, retention and deletion, portability, breach notification.

Draft 2026-10-04, for agreement with Chris Ruf by **2026-10-14** (charter step 1).

## What this document is

A Baylor best-practices document that puts the NCAA SSI *Performance Technologies
Recommendations: Responsible Use in Collegiate Athletics* (CSMAS/SSI, March 2026) into
practice in four areas Chris signs off on:

1. Technology adoption plan
2. Athlete consent
3. Vendor data contracts

Everything below assumes the recommendation in each. If he picks the other option,
the outline changes, but the schedule doesn't.

| # | Decision | Recommendation | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Best-practice guide or formal department policy? | **Guide plus procedures and forms**, with a one-page policy statement only if Chris wants one | At the 2026-07-30 meeting, leadership preferred "flexible best-practice documents over rigid formal policy". ## Proposed outline of the document

0. **Purpose and scope.** SSI basis, definitions (SSI's own, as UT does), who it applies to.
1. **Governance.** A standing Performance Technology Working Group: multidisciplinary, with student-athlete members (SSI Rec 1.1). Annual review of this document. Named owner. Medical authority over return-to-play stays with Athletic Medicine (Rec 3.3).

   - Annual re-consent, and re-consent when a new technology is introduced.
   - Where consent records live.
   - Annual education by group (Rec 2.1–2.3).
4. **Data management.**
   - Ownership, storage, access, and who may interpret and communicate data (Rec 3, 3.1).

   - Collect only what is used ("if you're not doing anything with it, don't collect it").
   - Transfer-athlete protocol (Rec 3.2).
5. **Vendor data contracts.**

Hands Free Body Weight Squat:

Starting position:

standing posture.

Arms extended out from the shoulder keeping them fixed for each rep.

Feet shoulder width apart.

ForceDecks protocol:

Ask individual to assume starting position.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight.

Stabilize individual – Instruct the individual to remain completely still, for 2-3 seconds before, and between each rep.

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform squat rep then resume the starting position.

Repeat squat for desired number of reps.

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Starting position:

Partial squat position / quarter-squat position.

Hands on hips.

Chest up and looking forward.

ForceDecks protocol:

Assume starting position – Ask individual to assume starting position.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight.

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform jump - Instruct the individual to:

Lower into a squat position above parallel depth.

Hold position, keeping chest up and hands on hips, for 3 seconds.

Jump up.

Land softly.

Assume starting position again.

Repeat jump for desired number of reps.

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Countermovement Jump

Starting position:

Normal standing posture.

Hands on hips (if unweighted) or hands on barbell (if weighted).

Chest up and looking forward.

ForceDecks protocol:

Assume starting position – Ask the individual to assume starting position on the plates.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform jump – Instruct the individual to:

Keep the chest up and looking forward.

Bend down.

Jump up.

Land softly.

Assume starting position again.

Repeat jump total of 3 countermovement jumps.

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Hop Test (Repeated CMJ Test)

Starting position:

Normal standing posture.

Hands on hips.

Chest up and looking forward.

ForceDecks protocol:

Assume starting position – Ask individual to assume starting position.

Weigh individual – Click “Weigh Athlete”. The individual must remain completely still, and the color display must register green before accepting body weight.

Stabilize individual – Instruct the athlete/client to remain completely still, in the standing position for 2-3 seconds before the first jump.

Start recording – Click “Start Recording”.

Perform jump – Instruct the individual to:

Keep chest up and looking forward.

Bend down.

Jump up.

Land stiff-legged on only the toes.

Quickly jump off the toes, for the desired number of reps, in rapid succession (safely keeping the knees as straight as possible).

Stop recording – Click “Stop Recording”.

Analyze – Click “Analyze and Save”.

Single Leg Countermovement Jump

Starting position:

Normal standing posture.

Hands on hips (if unweighted) or hands on barbell (if weighted).

Chest up and looking forward.

Land softly using only the desired leg for testing.

# Force Plate Practitioner course closeout — 2026-09-28

## Purpose and state

Archived the Applied Performance Force Plate Practitioner course for offline use and prepared its bibliography and resources in Zotero. The course capture and Zotero import are complete on the Windows machine. Direct Flint ingestion was not part of the verified closeout.

## Verified deliverables

- Drive archive: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\Force_Plate_Practitioner`. It has 76 lesson sets, each with one MP4, checked transcript, and summary, across 14 sections; 9 course PDF resources; 8 offline article Markdown files; and the README and course resource index. The delivery script checked copied file hashes.
- Zotero collection: `Force Plate Practitioner`, key `AE56U77Q`. The live local API showed 71 top-level records on 2026-09-27. The original import package covered 43 new course bibliography records and 9 course PDF records; the collection also holds other records.

CLEMSON OLYMPIC SPORTS SCIENCE POLICIES 
SOCIAL MEDIA  
Social media is a great tool for an aspiring sports scientist. On platforms such as 
Twitter or Instagram, there are many opportunities to learn from, and connect with, 
practitioners, researchers, S&C coaches, and fellow sports scientists in the field. 
However, you must be mindful and strategic in your social media presence. The 
content you produce is a direct reflection of Clemson University, the Clemson Athletic 
Department, and Clemson Olympic S&C and Sports Science.  
1. If you would like to share content related to Clemson S&C and Sports Science,

2. Never post any confidential, sensitive, personal, or proprietary information 
about Clemson student-athletes.  
3. Obey social media bylaws, including those laws governing defamation,

4. Remember: social media posts are immediate, permanent, and never truly

STUDENT-ATHLETE INTERACTIONS 
As a member of Clemson S&C and Sports Science, you will be interacting with

boundaries between you and Clemson student-athletes in the work and outside

VIOLATION OF THESE POLICY GUIDELINES MAY BE GROUNDS FOR IMMEDIATE

Last update: 3/17/2022 
CLEMSON OLYMPIC SPORTS SCIENCE PRINCIPLES 
The Clemson Olympic Sports Science team functions to meet six principles to offer 
support across the Athletic Department. These principles allow the high-performance 
team (S&C, sports medicine, nutrition, sports psychology, and coaching staffs) the 
ability to: 
• Answer team- and/or technology-specific questions 
• Ask better questions based upon presented evidence 
• Discover new questions 
Below is a description of the six Clemson Olympic Sports Science principles. It is 
worth noting these principles are interrelated to provide maximal effectiveness. 
1) Athlete Readiness and Load Monitoring 
Clemson Olympic sports utilizes various subjective and objective measures related 
to health and performance across each season phase (pre-season, in-season, 
post-season, and off-season). Readiness and load monitoring data support the 
S&C and sports medicine staffs to determine appropriate training and return-to-
performance periodization with reference to typical training and match demands. 
2) Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance 
The high-performance team identifies sport- and position-specific key 
performance indicators (KPIs). Athlete evaluations (both clinical and performance-
based) are conducted at various times throughout the season for diagnostic 
screening (i.e., dynamic injury risk), performance testing, and KPI threshold 
identification. These evaluations, along with continued measures of athlete 
readiness and load monitoring, assist the sports medicine and S&C staffs by 
objectively monitoring return-to-performance progression.  
3) Performance Team Collaboration 
A main function of sports science is to “glue” together all members of the high-
performance team through effective knowledge dissemination. Data and 
information collected by one performance unit is valuable to other units for 
ensuring collaborative efforts. It is extremely important to note that sports science 
does not replace decision-making. Rather, sports science provides data and 
information to inform the decision-making process. 
 
3

Last update: 3/17/2022 
4) Data Integration and Analytics 
Clemson Olympic sports possess the resources to collect data from various 
sources. To provide holistic insight into athlete evaluation and monitoring, the 
sports science team makes conscious efforts to centralize and standardize athlete 
reporting. While most Clemson Olympic sports technology utilizes cloud-based 
applications for data storage, it is important that the sports science team 
integrates these data streams into an effective and efficient reporting outcome.  
When tasked by members of the high-performance team to answer deeper-level 
questions, the sports science team performs more sophisticated statistical and 
analytical techniques. These analyses are often accompanied by large datasets to 
provide better understanding of historical trends and predictive modeling. 
5) Systems and Principles 
Each member of the high-performance team utilizes specific models for athlete 
development, monitoring, and clinical care. The sports science team supports 
these processes through collaborative efforts to determine best practices for KPI 
collection and reporting throughout the season. Appreciation for the technical, 
tactical, physiological, biomechanical, and psychological demands of each sport 
will ensure the sports scientist is effectively contributing to the working model.  
6) Experimental Frontiers 
Internal research and development are important aspects for technology and data 
validation. Conducting formal research within Clemson Olympic sports offers the 
sports science community with information and data generalizable to highly skilled 
collegiate athletes. This research output may provide high-performance team 
members with knowledge to implement best practices for improving athlete 
performance and minimizing injury risk.

CLEMSON OLYMPIC SPORTS SCIENCE PRINCIPLES 
The Clemson Olympic Sports Science team functions to meet six principles to offer 
support across the Athletic Department. These principles allow the high-performance 
team (S&C, sports medicine, nutrition, sports psychology, and coaching staffs) the 
ability to: 
• Answer team- and/or technology-specific questions 
• Ask better questions based upon presented evidence 
• Discover new questions 
Below is a description of the six Clemson Olympic Sports Science principles. It is 
worth noting these principles are interrelated to provide maximal effectiveness. 
1) Athlete Readiness and Load Monitoring 
Clemson Olympic sports utilizes various subjective and objective measures related 
to health and performance across each season phase (pre-season, in-season, 
post-season, and off-season). Readiness and load monitoring data support the 
S&C and sports medicine staffs to determine appropriate training and return-to-
performance periodization with reference to typical training and match demands. 
2) Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance 
The high-performance team identifies sport- and position-specific key 
performance indicators (KPIs). Athlete evaluations (both clinical and performance-
based) are conducted at various times throughout the season for diagnostic 
screening (i.e., dynamic injury risk), performance testing, and KPI threshold 
identification. These evaluations, along with continued measures of athlete 
readiness and load monitoring, assist the sports medicine and S&C staffs by 
objectively monitoring return-to-performance progression.  
3) Performance Team Collaboration 
A main function of sports science is to “glue” together all members of the high-
performance team through effective knowledge dissemination. Data and 
information collected by one performance unit is valuable to other units for 
ensuring collaborative efforts. It is extremely important to note that sports science 
does not replace decision-making. Rather, sports science provides data and 
information to inform the decision-making process.

4) Data Integration and Analytics 
Clemson Olympic sports possess the resources to collect data from various 
sources. To provide holistic insight into athlete evaluation and monitoring, the 
sports science team makes conscious efforts to centralize and standardize athlete 
reporting. While most Clemson Olympic sports technology utilizes cloud-based 
applications for data storage, it is important that the sports science team 
integrates these data streams into an effective and efficient reporting outcome.  
When tasked by members of the high-performance team to answer deeper-level 
questions, the sports science team performs more sophisticated statistical and 
analytical techniques. These analyses are often accompanied by large datasets to 
provide better understanding of historical trends and predictive modeling. 
5) Systems and Principles 
Each member of the high-performance team utilizes specific models for athlete 
development, monitoring, and clinical care. The sports science team supports 
these processes through collaborative efforts to determine best practices for KPI 
collection and reporting throughout the season. Appreciation for the technical, 
tactical, physiological, biomechanical, and psychological demands of each sport 
will ensure the sports scientist is effectively contributing to the working model.  
6) Experimental Frontiers 
Internal research and development are important aspects for technology and data 
validation. Conducting formal research within Clemson Olympic sports offers the 
sports science community with information and data generalizable to highly skilled 
collegiate athletes. This research output may provide high-performance team 
members with knowledge to implement best practices for improving athlete 
performance and minimizing injury risk.

speed, power, and rotational characteristics of a batter’s swing. 
Force Hooks 
Purpose: Dynamometry devices to measure force and isometric strength. 
Hawkin Dynamics

GymAware

# GPS & Force Plate Data Repository
**Context for Claude Code**

I'm building a centralized database for athletic performance data at Baylor University. The two primary data sources are Catapult GPS (player load, distance, velocity zones) and VALD ForceDecks (CMJ force plate metrics). This project has been started and stopped several times due to unresolved architecture decisions and API friction.

---

## Decisions Already Made
Do not revisit these.

- **Scope:** Single sport project database first, not department-wide infrastructure
- **Starting data type:** TBD at session start (likely Football GPS or ForceDecks)
- **API approach:** Start with manual CSV exports, layer in live API connections once the data model is stable
- **Storage preference:** SQLite or DuckDB to start (no IT dependency, runs locally, easy to migrate later)

---

## Technical Environment

- Windows machine
- Comfortable in Python and R
- Power BI for dashboards
- Baylor IT constraints mean cloud-hosted solutions need approval before use
- Previous API attempts with Catapult and ForceDecks have stalled

---

## What I Want to Build

A queryable local database that holds historical GPS and force plate data, supports one repeatable report or query as the MVP, and can eventually feed into Power BI dashboards. The end goal is owning the data pipeline rather than relying solely on vendor platforms.

---

## What I Do Not Want

- Over-engineered solutions
- Cloud infrastructure that requires IT approval to get started
- Anything that breaks and can't be fixed in-season without significant effort

---

## How to Work With Me

1. Start by confirming which sport and data type we are targeting this session
2. Help me define the one MVP query before writing any code
3. Ask about my actual CSV export format before designing the schema -- Catapult and ForceDecks exports have specific column structures we need to work around

---

# SSI crosswalk: Draft v1 of the guide

Every statement in the NCAA SSI *Performance Technologies Recommendations: Responsible
Use in Collegiate Athletics* (CSMAS/SSI, March 2026), mapped to the section or appendix of
`deliverables/SSI_BestPractices_GUIDE_DRAFTv1_ER_2026-10-04` that meets it. SSI item text
is summarised from `docs/SOURCES.md` § B. Status: **Met** = the guide carries it in full;
**Met, pending** = carried, but a position in it waits on the review named in
`docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`.

Guide sections: 0 Purpose and scope · 1 Governance · 2 Technology adoption · 3 Athlete
consent and education · 4 Data management · 5 Vendor data contracts · 6 Staff-transition
continuity · 7 Continuous improvement. Appendices: A Consent · B Vendor checklist ·
C Offboarding · D Annual review · E Technology intake.

## Foundational statements (SSI p2)

| SSI item | What SSI asks | Where the guide meets it | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 Fundamentals: broad definition | Performance technology covers devices, cameras, sensors, surveys, software and apps | §0 Definitions (SSI definition adopted verbatim in substance; scope lists video, surveys and apps) | Met |
| F1 Fundamentals: "just one tool" | Technology supports, never replaces, professional judgment | §0 Principles ("data guided, not data driven"); §4.4 interpretation rule | Met |
| F1 Fundamentals: quality varies | Assess accuracy, reliability, validity, function before selecting | §2 and Appendix E (gates and rated features) | Met |
| F2 Rights and protections | Know student-athlete rights, local and international law; watch for unintended impacts including mental health | §3 (notice vs consent, rights list), §3.5 education topics, §4.1 legal basis including international law, §7 survey items on harm; Appendix A rights section | Met, pending (OGC: legal classification) |
| F3 Written plan | A plan for education, data management, purchase decisions and continuous improvement | The guide itself, with §1 naming owner, review and version control | Met, pending (Chris: owner and sign-off) |

## Recommendation 1: Policy

| SSI item | What SSI asks | Where the guide meets it | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rec 1 | Establish a written plan | The guide (§0–§7) plus forms A–E | Met |
| 1.1 | Multidisciplinary team, including student-athletes, develops and routinely reviews the plan | §1.1 Working Group membership (two student-athletes, Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, coaches, administration, OGC, ITS, Compliance); §1.3 annual review; Appendix D | Met, pending (Chris: charter the group) |

# Applied Performance Digest: sources

Read 2026-10-04. Every source the Digest draws on, with what each one contributes. Source
files stay where they are (Drive or repo root); none of them are copied into `docs/`.
No login credentials, staff names from other schools, or athlete data are reproduced here.

Rule for borrowing: Clemson and Iowa give structure and ideas. Baylor gives content, voice
and brand. Nothing from Clemson or Iowa is quoted into Digest chapters.

## Baylor documents (the base)

### 1. Baylor Applied Performance Playbook, current version (Nov 2025 docx)

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\99_UNSORTED\From_External\Performance Play Book\Baylor Applied Performance Playbook.docx`
- Dates: created 2024-05-14, last modified 2025-11-10 (file metadata). Author field names a Baylor staff member.
- Size: 890 paragraphs, 1 table, about 10,300 words. No page count (Word file).
- Internal title: "Baylor Athletics Applied Performance Operations Guide."

What it contributes: the base text for the handbook and the ops manual. Sections: Preparing
Champions for Life, One Standard One Accord, Health and Wellness unit missions (Athletic
Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, Mental Health Services), Applied
Performance mission and four operating principles, technology overview (11 entries), login
placeholders (no credentials filled in), technology workflows for Catapult, DynaMo,
ForceDecks, ForceFrame, NordBord, Perch, Polar and SmartSpeed, and a vendor-level data
dictionary (Catapult parameters, Perch VBT metrics, ForceDecks jump metrics). The Catapult
workflow is written from practice; the VALD, Perch, Polar and SmartSpeed workflows follow one
generic template. The ForceDecks section is short: a settings checklist, a queue-based test
sequence, and a link to the vendor protocol list. There is no troubleshooting anywhere.

Version check against the May 2024 PDF: the docx is the newer file by date, but the two are
97.5 percent identical at word level (10,272 vs 10,330 words). The only differences are the
PDF's table of contents, the position of the technology overview table, and one dropped
phrase in a participant registration step. Treat the content as unchanged since May 2024.
Everything the Feb 2026 gap analysis says about the Baylor document still applies.

### 2. Baylor Applied Performance Playbook, May 2024 PDF

- Path: repo root, `Baylor Applied Performance Playbook.pdf`
- Dates: created and modified 2024-05-20.
- Size: 27 pages, about 10,400 words.

What it contributes: the dated snapshot the Feb 2026 gap analysis was written against, and
the page-numbered reference when a chapter needs to cite "the current guide." Use the docx
for text, this PDF for page references.

### 3. Revised Force Plate Testing V3 (Baylor protocol)

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\99_UNSORTED\From_Desktop\SPORT_SCIENCE\PROTOCOLS\FORCE PLATES\Revised Force Plate Testing V3.docx` (text copy indexed by the Flint project)
- Date: unknown; author uncertain (see Memory and notes).
- Size: about 885 words.

What it contributes: Baylor's own step-by-step ForceDecks protocol. Two testing conditions
(inside a training session with the team warm-up, or outside a session with a standard
three-drill warm-up). Scripted steps for each test: assume position, weigh until the display
registers green, stand still 2 to 3 seconds, Start Recording, perform reps, Stop Recording,
Analyze and Save. Rep counts: hands-free squat x3, squat jump x3, CMJ x3, hop test 10 reps,
single-leg CMJ x3 per leg, plus an isometric seated calf raise run on the Mid-Thigh Pull
setting. This is the primary source for chapter 1. Note that it uses button names
("Weigh Athlete," "Start Recording") that differ from the Operations Guide ("Weigh Start,"
"Play"), which points to two different ForceDecks app versions.

### 4. Technology SOP template

- Paths: `TechnologyTemplateSOP.pdf` (repo root, 4 pages, about 450 words) and its text version `docs/program/Technology_SOP_Template.md`.
- Date: PDF metadata 2018-11-21; placed in the repo 2026-02-16.

What it contributes: the section skeleton for every ops-manual chapter: header block with
contacts, equipment inventory with photos, setup location, charging, preparing the athlete,
software operations, running a test, data management and export with a file naming
convention, teardown and storage, troubleshooting table, key metrics table, vendor support
table, revision history. Chapter 1 follows this skeleton.

### 5. Performance Playbook Development Plan (Feb 2026 gap analysis)

- Path: repo root, `Performance_Playbook_Development_Plan.docx`
- Dates: created 2026-02-16, modified 2026-02-25.
- Size: 103 paragraphs, 3 tables, about 2,700 words.

What it contributes: the Clemson-vs-Baylor comparison the Digest builds on. Five gap
categories (no intern curriculum, no sport-specific data dictionaries, no daily checklists,
generic workflows, no principles or policies), a strengths list, a three-phase action plan,
a 16-week intern curriculum table, and a recommended 14-section final structure. The Digest
outline is this 14-section structure regrouped under three parts, with Iowa and NCAA
material added. See `gap-update.md` for what still holds.

## Structural inspiration

### 6. Clemson Olympic Sports Science Playbook (Spring 2023)

- Path: repo root, `Clemson OLY Sports Science Playbook (Spring 2023_NoIntern.pdf`
- Dates: pages carry "last update" stamps from March to November 2022; the PDF was assembled 2026-02-14.
- Size: 98 pages, about 21,700 words. Roughly pages 45 to 85 are vendor material (Moxy monitor ebooks), not Clemson writing. The 173-page intern curriculum is a separate file (`IntenCurriculumn.pdf`, 26 MB, not read for this pass).

What it contributes: the shape of a department playbook that doubles as an onboarding
manual. Order: introduction and expectations, policies (social media, student-athlete
interactions), six principles with narrative descriptions, a daily intern checklist listing
each device by name for morning and evening charging, a dated 16-week intern schedule tied to
NSCA textbook chapters, technology overview with a one-line purpose per device, a data
dictionary organized by sport, and a workflow per device in a fixed pattern: setup,
testing the athlete, troubleshooting, data management, links. The workflows name the
specific device IDs, the storage location ("back office") and the exact app buttons. Its
login section lists credentials in plain text, which is a security problem the Baylor guide
rightly avoided; the Digest keeps placeholders and points to a credential vault.

## Assessment and testing inspiration

### 7. University of Iowa Sports Performance Assessment Manual

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\99_UNSORTED\From_External\Performance Play Book\IA ASSESSEMENT MANUAL.pdf`
- Dates: file saved 2024-05-15; PDF metadata created 2017-08-21, modified 2022-04-08.
- Size: 27 pages, about 5,100 words. Page 9 (the sport assessment table) and page 21 are images with no extractable text.

What it contributes: the model for how to write a testing procedure. Front matter on why
to test, specific vs general tests, validity types, reliability (interrater, intrarater,
3 to 4 familiarization trials), detecting change (smallest meaningful change), when to
reassess (phase of season, expected change, known fatigue), menstrual cycle considerations,
and athlete preparation rules (carbohydrate intake 36 hours out, no food or caffeine 2 hours
before, no severe fatigue 48 to 72 hours before, same time of day, fixed test order). Then
one entry per test in a fixed pattern: description, how to test, frequency by purpose,
validity and reliability, interpretation with numbers, equipment. Its CMJ entry gives hands
on hips, jump as high as possible with no strategy coaching, stiff landing, three jumps,
and frequency rules for asymmetry, jump height, and RSImod. Limits: it is written for
Athletic Performance coaches, its stack is 2017-era (GymAware, contact mats, FreeLap), it
has no software steps, a few Frequency sections are empty, and it names a staff member in
two places.

### 8. 2017-11-06 UIowa Performance Manual

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\08_ADMIN\Policy_Procedure\2017-11-06_UIowa_Performance_Manual.pdf`
- Dates: file saved 2017-11-16; PDF metadata 2017-08-21.
- Size: 27 pages, about 5,100 words.

Finding: identical text to source 7, byte for byte after extraction. The "May 2024" file is
a re-save of the 2017 manual, not a newer edition. Cite source 7 and treat the content as
2017.

## NCAA tech items

### 9. Performance Technology Best Practices guide (NCAA SSI), Draft v1

- Repo: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` (read only; not edited by this project)
- Guide: `deliverables/SSI_BestPractices_GUIDE_DRAFTv1_ER_2026-10-04.docx` and `.pdf`, 9 pages, sections 0 to 7.
- Forms A to E: consent, vendor data checklist, offboarding checklist, annual review, technology intake. 2 pages each.
- Supporting docs: `docs/PLAN.md` (three decisions for Chris Ruf, due 10/14), `docs/SSI_CROSSWALK.md` (all 24 SSI items mapped), `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md` (15 pending items with owners), `docs/SOURCES.md`.
- Date: 2026-10-04.

What it contributes: Part 3 of the Digest in full. The Digest links to this guide and its
forms rather than rewriting them. Guide sections: purpose and scope, governance (a working
group with student-athlete members), technology adoption (points to the Software and
Technology Management Framework request process), athlete consent and education, data
management, vendor data contracts, staff-transition continuity, continuous improvement. The
guide assumes three decisions Chris has not yet made (guide vs policy; this guide as the
framework's Version 1; four areas plus a short education section). If he decides otherwise,
sections 0 to 2 change, so the Digest's Part 3 stays a link until after 10/14.

## Memory and notes

Facts recalled through `memsearch` (six queries: "Applied Performance Digest", "performance
playbook", "ForceDecks CMJ procedure", "intern curriculum", "Technology SOP template", "NCAA
best practices performance technology") and two RunningTheRoom documents. These set the
audience, scope and deadlines; none of them are vendor or peer-school text.

- **The Digest and its deadline.** RunningTheRoom `docs/STATUS.md` and
  `docs/handoffs/2026-09-25-answers-self-audit-myelin-cleanup.md`: the Applied Performance
  Digest has three parts (handbook, ops manual, NCAA tech items). Chapter 1 is the ForceDecks
  CMJ procedure, due 10/23, third item in the ship queue after Research in 5 #002 (week of
  9/28) and intern curriculum Module 1 (10/9). Stick checks about 10/28, 11/8, 11/22.
- **The D1 rule.** Same handoff: ship one piece every two weeks to a named user, log it in
  the status report "Shipped" section, run a 30-day "still using it?" check. The self-audit
  finding behind it: the one change that stuck had a daily-user co-owner; the five that faded
  were solo. Chapter 1 therefore needs a named daily user before it ships.
- **Baylor's CMJ practice** (Flint `method-baseline.md`, from the 2026-09-28 interview and
  SportSmith notes): force plate CMJ is the department's long-running longitudinal tool.
  Modified RSI from CMJ testing is the daily readiness marker, read on Wednesdays against
  individualized thresholds (percent change from baseline, rolling average, SD and smallest
  worthwhile change). Daily jumps build the baseline; Wednesday is the decision read. The
  dynamic strength index (CMJ peak force over IMTP peak force) steers plyometric vs
  max-strength emphasis; tagged contested in the evidence check.
- **Metric selection framework** (same file, origin Hawkin Dynamics, adopted practice): 1 to
  2 output metrics, 1 to 3 driver metrics, 1 to 3 strategy metrics, optional symmetry, and
  "fluffy" metrics only with a stated reason.
- **The V3 protocol's status** (same file): the CMJ family and rep counts are marked
  "inferred, author uncertain." Chapter 1 asks Eric to confirm V3 is the live protocol.
- **NordBord** (same file): roster-wide football NordBord testing was retired after January
  2023; kept only for small return-to-play groups. The Operations Guide still documents the
  full roster SOP. The Digest's NordBord chapter must reflect current practice.
- **Intern curriculum is not built** (same file, Eric, 2026-09-28, Q30). It is a separate
  project (`Intern_Curriculum`) with its own 10/9 deadline. The Digest references it and does
  not absorb it, which matches the Feb 2026 plan's section 5.3.
- **Leadership prefers flexible guidance** (2026-07-30 Applied Performance meeting note in
  SecondBrain): best-practice documents over rigid formal policy. The NCAA plan's decision 1
  follows this.
- **Protocol drift** (SecondBrain, Old Bull performance course note): a test can keep its
  name while the procedure changes underneath it, and the data cannot show you. The reason
  chapter 1 fixes cues, rep counts and settings in writing.
- **ForceDecks data flow** (`cmj-traffic-light` plan; `ForcePlate_DecisionSystem` spec;
  `DataBase_GPS_Reporting` context): current practice exports CSV from ForceDecks or pulls
  from the VALD API into a local DuckDB; Kitman Labs is the athlete management system of
  record per the Operations Guide. Chapter 1 marks the live export path as a confirm item.
- **Baylor technology stack** (Feb 2026 plan, section 5.3): ForceDecks, Catapult,
  ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar. Clemson devices not at Baylor
  (1080 Sprint, Proteus, Moxy, MuscleLab, PlyoMat, GymAware, Hawkin Dynamics) are not
  covered.

## Not found or not read

- **"AP Assessment Manual V12"**: named in the Flint provenance note as a Baylor document
  with uncertain authorship. Not located on disk or Drive in this pass. If it exists, it
  belongs in the handbook part next to the Iowa-derived assessment chapter.
- **`IntenCurriculumn.pdf`** (Clemson intern curriculum, 173 pages, 26 MB): in the repo root,
  not read. It belongs to the Intern_Curriculum project, not the Digest.
- **Clemson page 9 table and Iowa page 9 and 21**: images without extractable text. Not
  needed for this pass.

Read 2026-10-04. Every source the Digest draws on, with what each one contributes. Source
files stay where they are (Drive or repo root); none of them are copied into `docs/`.
No login credentials, staff names from other schools, or athlete data are reproduced here.

Rule for borrowing: Clemson and Iowa give structure and ideas. Baylor gives content, voice
and brand. Nothing from Clemson or Iowa is quoted into Digest chapters.

## Baylor documents (the base)

### 1. Baylor Applied Performance Playbook, current version (Nov 2025 docx)

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\99_UNSORTED\From_External\Performance Play Book\Baylor Applied Performance Playbook.docx`
- Dates: created 2024-05-14, last modified 2025-11-10 (file metadata). Author field names a Baylor staff member.
- Size: 890 paragraphs, 1 table, about 10,300 words. No page count (Word file).
- Internal title: "Baylor Athletics Applied Performance Operations Guide."

What it contributes: the base text for the handbook and the ops manual. Sections: Preparing
Champions for Life, One Standard One Accord, Health and Wellness unit missions (Athletic
Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, Mental Health Services), Applied
Performance mission and four operating principles, technology overview (11 entries), login
placeholders (no credentials filled in), technology workflows for Catapult, DynaMo,
ForceDecks, ForceFrame, NordBord, Perch, Polar and SmartSpeed, and a vendor-level data
dictionary (Catapult parameters, Perch VBT metrics, ForceDecks jump metrics). The Catapult
workflow is written from practice; the VALD, Perch, Polar and SmartSpeed workflows follow one
generic template. The ForceDecks section is short: a settings checklist, a queue-based test
sequence, and a link to the vendor protocol list. There is no troubleshooting anywhere.

Version check against the May 2024 PDF: the docx is the newer file by date, but the two are
97.5 percent identical at word level (10,272 vs 10,330 words). The only differences are the
PDF's table of contents, the position of the technology overview table, and one dropped
phrase in a participant registration step. Treat the content as unchanged since May 2024.
Everything the Feb 2026 gap analysis says about the Baylor document still applies.

### 2. Baylor Applied Performance Playbook, May 2024 PDF

- Path: repo root, `Baylor Applied Performance Playbook.pdf`
- Dates: created and modified 2024-05-20.
- Size: 27 pages, about 10,400 words.

What it contributes: the dated snapshot the Feb 2026 gap analysis was written against, and
the page-numbered reference when a chapter needs to cite "the current guide." Use the docx
for text, this PDF for page references.

### 3. Revised Force Plate Testing V3 (Baylor protocol)

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\99_UNSORTED\From_Desktop\SPORT_SCIENCE\PROTOCOLS\FORCE PLATES\Revised Force Plate Testing V3.docx` (text copy indexed by the Flint project)
- Date: unknown; author uncertain (see Memory and notes).
- Size: about 885 words.

What it contributes: Baylor's own step-by-step ForceDecks protocol. Two testing conditions
(inside a training session with the team warm-up, or outside a session with a standard
three-drill warm-up). Scripted steps for each test: assume position, weigh until the display
registers green, stand still 2 to 3 seconds, Start Recording, perform reps, Stop Recording,
Analyze and Save. Rep counts: hands-free squat x3, squat jump x3, CMJ x3, hop test 10 reps,
single-leg CMJ x3 per leg, plus an isometric seated calf raise run on the Mid-Thigh Pull
setting. This is the primary source for chapter 1. Note that it uses button names
("Weigh Athlete," "Start Recording") that differ from the Operations Guide ("Weigh Start,"
"Play"), which points to two different ForceDecks app versions.

### 4. Technology SOP template

- Paths: `TechnologyTemplateSOP.pdf` (repo root, 4 pages, about 450 words) and its text version `docs/program/Technology_SOP_Template.md`.
- Date: PDF metadata 2018-11-21; placed in the repo 2026-02-16.

What it contributes: the section skeleton for every ops-manual chapter: header block with
contacts, equipment inventory with photos, setup location, charging, preparing the athlete,
software operations, running a test, data management and export with a file naming
convention, teardown and storage, troubleshooting table, key metrics table, vendor support
table, revision history. Chapter 1 follows this skeleton.

### 5. Performance Playbook Development Plan (Feb 2026 gap analysis)

- Path: repo root, `Performance_Playbook_Development_Plan.docx`
- Dates: created 2026-02-16, modified 2026-02-25.
- Size: 103 paragraphs, 3 tables, about 2,700 words.

What it contributes: the Clemson-vs-Baylor comparison the Digest builds on. Five gap
categories (no intern curriculum, no sport-specific data dictionaries, no daily checklists,
generic workflows, no principles or policies), a strengths list, a three-phase action plan,
a 16-week intern curriculum table, and a recommended 14-section final structure. The Digest
outline is this 14-section structure regrouped under three parts, with Iowa and NCAA
material added. See `gap-update.md` for what still holds.

## Structural inspiration

### 6. Clemson Olympic Sports Science Playbook (Spring 2023)

- Path: repo root, `Clemson OLY Sports Science Playbook (Spring 2023_NoIntern.pdf`
- Dates: pages carry "last update" stamps from March to November 2022; the PDF was assembled 2026-02-14.
- Size: 98 pages, about 21,700 words. Roughly pages 45 to 85 are vendor material (Moxy monitor ebooks), not Clemson writing. The 173-page intern curriculum is a separate file (`IntenCurriculumn.pdf`, 26 MB, not read for this pass).

What it contributes: the shape of a department playbook that doubles as an onboarding
manual. Order: introduction and expectations, policies (social media, student-athlete
interactions), six principles with narrative descriptions, a daily intern checklist listing
each device by name for morning and evening charging, a dated 16-week intern schedule tied to
NSCA textbook chapters, technology overview with a one-line purpose per device, a data
dictionary organized by sport, and a workflow per device in a fixed pattern: setup,
testing the athlete, troubleshooting, data management, links. The workflows name the
specific device IDs, the storage location ("back office") and the exact app buttons. Its
login section lists credentials in plain text, which is a security problem the Baylor guide
rightly avoided; the Digest keeps placeholders and points to a credential vault.

## Assessment and testing inspiration

### 7. University of Iowa Sports Performance Assessment Manual

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\99_UNSORTED\From_External\Performance Play Book\IA ASSESSEMENT MANUAL.pdf`
- Dates: file saved 2024-05-15; PDF metadata created 2017-08-21, modified 2022-04-08.
- Size: 27 pages, about 5,100 words. Page 9 (the sport assessment table) and page 21 are images with no extractable text.

What it contributes: the model for how to write a testing procedure. Front matter on why
to test, specific vs general tests, validity types, reliability (interrater, intrarater,
3 to 4 familiarization trials), detecting change (smallest meaningful change), when to
reassess (phase of season, expected change, known fatigue), menstrual cycle considerations,
and athlete preparation rules (carbohydrate intake 36 hours out, no food or caffeine 2 hours
before, no severe fatigue 48 to 72 hours before, same time of day, fixed test order). Then
one entry per test in a fixed pattern: description, how to test, frequency by purpose,
validity and reliability, interpretation with numbers, equipment. Its CMJ entry gives hands
on hips, jump as high as possible with no strategy coaching, stiff landing, three jumps,
and frequency rules for asymmetry, jump height, and RSImod. Limits: it is written for
Athletic Performance coaches, its stack is 2017-era (GymAware, contact mats, FreeLap), it
has no software steps, a few Frequency sections are empty, and it names a staff member in
two places.

### 8. 2017-11-06 UIowa Performance Manual

- Path: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\08_ADMIN\Policy_Procedure\2017-11-06_UIowa_Performance_Manual.pdf`
- Dates: file saved 2017-11-16; PDF metadata 2017-08-21.
- Size: 27 pages, about 5,100 words.

Finding: identical text to source 7, byte for byte after extraction. The "May 2024" file is
a re-save of the 2017 manual, not a newer edition. Cite source 7 and treat the content as
2017.

## NCAA tech items

### 9. Performance Technology Best Practices guide (NCAA SSI), Draft v1

- Repo: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` (read only; not edited by this project)
- Guide: `deliverables/SSI_BestPractices_GUIDE_DRAFTv1_ER_2026-10-04.docx` and `.pdf`, 9 pages, sections 0 to 7.
- Forms A to E: consent, vendor data checklist, offboarding checklist, annual review, technology intake. 2 pages each.
- Supporting docs: `docs/PLAN.md` (three decisions for Chris Ruf, due 10/14), `docs/SSI_CROSSWALK.md` (all 24 SSI items mapped), `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md` (15 pending items with owners), `docs/SOURCES.md`.
- Date: 2026-10-04.

What it contributes: Part 3 of the Digest in full. The Digest links to this guide and its
forms rather than rewriting them. Guide sections: purpose and scope, governance (a working
group with student-athlete members), technology adoption (points to the Software and
Technology Management Framework request process), athlete consent and education, data
management, vendor data contracts, staff-transition continuity, continuous improvement. The
guide assumes three decisions Chris has not yet made (guide vs policy; this guide as the
framework's Version 1; four areas plus a short education section). If he decides otherwise,
sections 0 to 2 change, so the Digest's Part 3 stays a link until after 10/14.

## Memory and notes

Facts recalled through `memsearch` (six queries: "Applied Performance Digest", "performance
playbook", "ForceDecks CMJ procedure", "intern curriculum", "Technology SOP template", "NCAA
best practices performance technology") and two RunningTheRoom documents. These set the

  CMJ procedure, due 10/23, third item in the ship queue after Research in 5 #002 (week of
  9/28) and intern curriculum Module 1 (10/9). Stick checks about 10/28, 11/8, 11/22.
- **The D1 rule.** Same handoff: ship one piece every two weeks to a named user, log it in
  the status report "Shipped" section, run a 30-day "still using it?" check. The self-audit

- **Leadership prefers flexible guidance** (2026-07-30 Applied Performance meeting note in

  record per the Operations Guide. Chapter 1 marks the live export path as a confirm item.
- **Baylor technology stack** (Feb 2026 plan, section 5.3): ForceDecks, Catapult,
  ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar. Clemson devices not at Baylor
  (1080 Sprint, Proteus, Moxy, MuscleLab, PlyoMat, GymAware, Hawkin Dynamics) are not
  covered.

## Not found or not read

- **"AP Assessment Manual V12"**: named in the Flint provenance note as a Baylor document

# Gap update: what the Feb 2026 plan still gets right, what changed, and the Iowa column

Written 2026-10-04. Builds on `Performance_Playbook_Development_Plan.docx` (Feb 2026,
Clemson vs Baylor). This does not redo that analysis. It checks it against the current
Baylor document, records what changed around it, and adds the comparison it lacked: Iowa.

## Short answer

The Feb 2026 plan still holds in full, because the Baylor document it analyzed has not
changed. The Nov 2025 docx is the May 2024 text with a few formatting edits (97.5 percent
identical at word level). What changed is everything around the document: the NCAA SSI
recommendations and Baylor's draft response to them, the two-week ship rule, the intern
curriculum becoming its own project, and one workflow (NordBord) that no longer matches
practice. Iowa adds one thing neither Clemson nor Baylor has: a written theory of testing
and a fixed per-test format that a coach can read without a software manual.

  transfer.

2. Does the Digest retire the Operations Guide docx, or do both live until the Digest covers

   without one will fade.
